concepts.name: Arabic Script Feature (A/1/3450)
concepts.summary: The paper's lead case study: a learned feature that fires on text in Arabic script, is specific and reasonably sensitive to it, and has no neuron counterpart.
concepts.explanation: A/1/3450 activates on text in Arabic, Farsi, Urdu and probably other languages written in the Arabic script. Arabic script is 0.13% of training tokens but 81% of tokens where the feature is active, and 98% above activation 5. Its logit weights have a second mode consisting of Arabic characters and the byte tokens \xd8 and \xd9 that begin the UTF-8 encodings of basic Arabic characters. Ablating it hurts predictions on Arabic tokens and helps prediction of shared punctuation such as the period. The three largest coefficients of this feature in the neuron basis are all negative, and the [[most-correlated-neuron]] responds to a mixture of non-English languages, so the paper concludes the feature would be effectively invisible in a neuron-level analysis.

sections.title: The feature is not a neuron

concepts.name: Automated Interpretability
concepts.summary: Having a language model write an explanation of a feature from examples where it activates, then use that explanation alone to predict the feature's activations on unseen tokens.
concepts.explanation: Following Bills et al., the paper uses Claude to generate an explanation of each feature from examples of where it fires, then, in a separate interaction, asks the model to predict activations on previously unseen tokens using only that explanation. The score is the correlation between predicted and true activations. The setup is designed so that no information about activation patterns leaks except through the explanation — when predicting, the model cannot see any true activations of that feature. The paper finds Claude explains and predicts features significantly better than neurons, agreeing with the human analysis, and it also applies the same explanations to a second task on logit weights.

citedFrom.refText: Bills, Steven and Cammarata, Nick and Mossing, Dan and Tillman, Henk and Gao, Leo and Goh, Gabriel and Sutskever, Ilya and Leike, Jan and Wu, Jeff and Saunders, William (2023). Language models can explain neurons in language models.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The explain-then-simulate protocol, the activation quantization, and the scoring scheme this paper adapts and deliberately deviates from are all specified there.

concepts.name: Computational Proxy
concepts.summary: A cheaply computable numerical score estimating how likely a string is to come from a hypothesized context, used as an independent yardstick against which feature activations are checked.
concepts.explanation: To test specificity and sensitivity without hand-labeling millions of tokens, the paper builds a proxy for each context: an estimate of the log-likelihood ratio $\log(P(s|\text{context}) / P(s))$, the probability of the string under the context hypothesis versus under the full empirical distribution of the dataset. The stated intuition for using log-likelihoods is that features interact linearly with the logits, so they should be incentivized to track log-likelihoods. Because a token's activation may depend on preceding tokens, the ratio is maximized over different prefixes leading up to and including the final token. The four contexts were chosen because they are easy to model: DNA as random strings over [ATCG], base64 as random sequences over [a-zA-Z0-9+/], and Arabic and Hebrew via their well-defined Unicode blocks.

concepts.name: Dictionary learning
concepts.summary: The problem of writing each activation vector as a sparse combination of directions drawn from a fixed, larger-than-necessary set. The paper frames the search for a model's features as exactly this problem.
concepts.explanation: Given activation vectors $\mathbf{x}$, dictionary learning looks for a set of directions $\mathbf{d}_i$ and per-datapoint coefficients $f_i(\mathbf{x})$ such that $\mathbf{x} \approx \sum_i f_i(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{d}_i$, with only a few coefficients nonzero on any given datapoint. The paper adopts this framing because it believes the features it is after are sparse and more numerous than the dimensions available to hold them. It asks only for a sparse decomposition of the activations themselves and uses nothing about what those activations go on to do in the rest of the model. The paper points out that this restraint is useful: because downstream effects were never fitted, they are left free to act as an independent check on whether the recovered directions mean anything.

citedFrom.refText: Elad, Michael (2010). Sparse and redundant representations: from theory to applications in signal and image processing.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The paper names sparse dictionary learning as a pre-existing problem and cites this book plus Olshausen & Field for the definition rather than restating it.

sections.title: Using Sparse Autoencoders To Find Good Decompositions
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: Telling Whether the Autoencoder Is Working
concepts.summary: The paper has no single metric that tracks what it cares about, and instead triangulates from several imperfect signals.
concepts.explanation: In most of machine learning a held-out loss settles whether a method works. Here it does not, because the goal is interpretable features and reconstruction error alone can be driven down by an uninterpretable dense solution. The paper reports spending considerable time looking for a satisfactory metric and not finding one; it fell back on a combination of [[manual-inspection]], [[feature-density]] statistics, reconstruction loss, and toy models with known ground truth. It is explicit that some of these signals are hard to read — features that looked senseless sometimes made sense on deeper inspection — and says it would be very helpful if better metrics for [[dictionary-learning]] solutions existed.

sections.title: How can we tell if the autoencoder is working?
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

concepts.name: Feature
concepts.summary: A basic interpretable direction in activation space — the unit the paper wants to decompose models into, in place of neurons.
concepts.explanation: The paper's working definition is deliberately operational: if linear directions in activation space are interpretable, there should be some 'basic set' of meaningful directions from which more complex ones are built, and those are features. Sometimes individual neurons happen to be such units; often they are not. The paper takes an agnostic stance on whether models are 'in some fundamental sense composed of features' or whether features are a convenient post-hoc description, though it says its universality results suggest features have some existence beyond individual models. Every feature in this paper has both an activation condition (when it fires) and a downstream action (what it makes the model predict).

concepts.name: The Five-Claim Feature Template
concepts.summary: The fixed set of five claims the paper tries to establish for each individual feature it studies in depth: specificity, sensitivity, downstream effect, non-correspondence to a neuron, and universality.
concepts.explanation: Section 3 sets out a standard evidence template and then applies it to four hand-picked features. For each one the paper argues that (1) when the feature is on, the hypothesized context is usually present; (2) when the context is present, the feature is usually on; (3) the feature causes downstream behavior that fits the interpretation; (4) no single neuron corresponds to the feature; and (5) a similar feature turns up when [[dictionary-learning]] is run on an independently trained model. The paper says the most important claim of the whole work is that dictionary learning extracts features more monosemantic than neurons, and this template is how it argues that claim case by case. Claims 1 through 3 are demonstrated using computational proxies for each context; claims 4 and 5 use neuron comparisons and a second training run.

concepts.name: Feature motifs
concepts.summary: The recurring kinds of features the paper finds: context features, token-in-context features, trigram features, sequence-memorizing features, and features readable as actions.
concepts.explanation: Rather than catalogue individual features, the paper names the categories that keep appearing. It offers a theoretical reason for the prevalence of the first two: attention heads can largely implement three-point functions with two inputs and an output, while MLP layers are well positioned to implement conjunctions over many tokens — of which context and [[token-in-context-features|token-in-context features]] are the extreme cases. The volume of token-in-context features in particular is described as striking and as not what the authors expected to find in a one-layer model.

concepts.name: Feature splitting
concepts.summary: The observation that as the autoencoder is made wider, single features divide into families of more specific features covering roughly the same territory.
concepts.explanation: Going from 512 features in A/0 to 4,096 in A/1 to 16,384 in A/2, the number of features specific to base64 goes from one to three to many more. A 2-D UMAP of the combined feature directions from all three runs shows tight clusters, confirming that the qualitative families correspond to small angles between dictionary vectors. The paper's proposed explanation is that there is some idealized set of '[[true-features]]' held in very tight superposition, and a size-limited dictionary returns features that cover approximately the same territory at the cost of being less specific. If that picture is right, choosing the '[[correct-number-of-features]]' matters less than it seems: different sizes give different resolutions on the same object.

concepts.name: Fraction of MLP Loss Recovered
concepts.summary: The measure and its headline number: splice the autoencoder's reconstruction back into the transformer in place of the real MLP activations, and 79% of the loss reduction the MLP provides survives for A/1, rising to 94.5% for the much larger A/5.
concepts.explanation: The measure works by substitution: replace the MLP activations with the autoencoder's reconstruction of them and see how much extra loss that costs, relative to the loss cost of zero-ablating the MLP entirely. For A/1 the extra loss is 21% of the zero-ablation loss, so 79% of the MLP's contribution is recovered. The penalty can be reduced by using more features or a lower [[l1-coefficient]] — A/5, with n_learned_sparse of 131,072 and an L1 coefficient of 0.004, recovers 94.5%. The paper says these numbers should be taken with a significant grain of salt, while also arguing that the individual feature analyses show the recovered loss is measuring something real.

sections.title: How much of the model does our interpretation explain?
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

concepts.name: Manual Human Analysis
concepts.summary: A blinded human annotator scoring 412 activation intervals across 162 features and neurons on an interpretability rubric; the paper's most-trusted metric.
concepts.explanation: The paper says it has no metric it trusts more than human judgment, so one of the authors, Adam Jermyn, scored features and neurons blind to which was which. Rather than scoring whole units, samples were drawn uniformly across activation intervals and each interval scored separately against the hypothesis suggested by the feature as a whole. In total 412 [[feature-activation]] intervals were scored across 162 features and neurons — the paper is explicit that this is a small sample, because the method is labor intensive. The median neuron scored 0, meaning the annotator could not form any hypothesis about it, while the median feature interval scored 12 out of a possible 14, meaning a confident, specific, consistent hypothesis that also made sense of the logit weights.

concepts.name: Do Features Tell Us About The Model Or The Data?
concepts.summary: The worry that dictionary learning on activations might be recovering correlations in the dataset rather than anything the model computes, and the paper's answers to it.
concepts.explanation: A model's activations reflect both the dataset's distribution and the way the model transforms it, so [[dictionary-learning]] on activations mixes the two. Correlations in the data can survive the first part of the model, and the paper concedes it is in theory possible that the features are artifacts of dataset correlations projected into a different space. It gives two answers. First, the randomized-weight model: dictionary learning there yields mostly single-token features and non-single-token features it cannot interpret, so the trained model's activations have richer structure than the token distribution alone. Second, the structural argument: the second half of the model — MLP down-projection and unembedding — is not an input to dictionary learning, so the interpretability of downstream effects must be a property of the model, and the paper checks this three ways with logit weights, ablation, and pinned sampling.

sections.title: Do features tell us about the model or the data?

concepts.name: The One-Layer Transformer Testbed
concepts.summary: The model under study: a one-layer transformer with a 128-dimensional residual stream and a 512-neuron ReLU MLP, overtrained on 100 billion Pile tokens.
concepts.explanation: The paper treats this model as a testbed for [[dictionary-learning]] rather than an object of interest in itself, and gives three reasons for the choice. Being small, it likely has fewer '[[true-features]]' than a larger model, so modest dictionaries might cover all of them, and small dictionaries are cheap enough to allow fast hyperparameter search. It can be heavily overtrained cheaply. And because there is only one layer, the effect of features on the output logits is approximately linear and therefore easy to analyze. The tradeoff, which the paper names, is that these same properties may make its results less likely to generalize to multilayer models.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Pearson Correlation
concepts.summary: The standard linear correlation coefficient between two variables, ranging from -1 to 1.
concepts.explanation: Used throughout the paper to compare a feature's activations with a proxy, with a neuron's activations, or with a feature from another run.

concepts.name: Polysemanticity
concepts.summary: A single neuron responding to a mixture of seemingly unrelated inputs, which makes it a poor unit for human understanding of the network.
concepts.explanation: The paper's opening problem: the most natural computational unit, the neuron, is often not a natural unit of meaning. It cites a neuron in Inception v1 that fires on both cat faces and car fronts, and reports a neuron in its own small language model that fires on a mixture of academic citations, English dialogue, HTTP requests, and Korean text. If neurons respond to unrelated things, statements about network behavior phrased in terms of individual neuron activity do not compose into an explanation. Superposition is one hypothesized cause, but the paper later argues it is not the only one.

concepts.name: Reading this paper's charts
concepts.summary: The handful of chart shapes this paper argues with, each explained once: why that shape was chosen, how to read it, and what it would look like if the claim it supports were false.
concepts.explanation: This paper makes the same kinds of measurement over and over - on the Arabic feature, then the DNA one, then base64, then Hebrew - and plots each the same way. That repetition is the point: once you can read one activation spectrum you can read all of them, and the comparison across cases is where the argument actually lives. Each page below takes one of those shapes and says what question forced it, how to get information out of it, and what a negative result would look like on it.

concepts.name: Spearman Rank Correlation
concepts.summary: Correlation computed on the ranks of values rather than the values themselves.
concepts.explanation: Used as the main [[automated-interpretability]] score because it only requires the model to get the ordering of activations right, not their exact magnitudes.

concepts.name: Superposition
concepts.summary: A hypothesized phenomenon in which a network represents more independent features than it has neurons, by giving each feature its own linear combination of neurons.
concepts.explanation: Stated formally, the hypothesis has two parts that the paper leans on. First, the feature directions form an overcomplete basis — more directions $\mathbf{d}_i$ than neurons. Second, the feature activations are sparse, because sparsity is what makes the [[noisy-simulation]] work. Together these make recovering the features mathematically identical to the classic problem of [[dictionary-learning]], which is the paper's whole method. By the end the authors say the experiments left them more confident that some version of the hypothesis is true, while also convinced that the specific form they inherited from Toy Models is incomplete.

concepts.name: Universality
concepts.summary: The question of whether the same features form across different models, and the paper's finding that they largely do.
concepts.explanation: Universality matters generally because it decides whether lessons from one model transfer, and specifically here because it bears on whether the extracted features are real. The paper's argument for the latter is careful: at minimum, universality shows the features are not arbitrary artifacts of the [[dictionary-learning]] process, or that if they come from that process it is in a consistent way. It also means features can be treated as replicable, recurring units of analysis. And it is the kind of observation one would expect if models really do represent a finite discrete set of features in superposition. The paper tests two strengths of the claim: across two identically-trained models, and against features reported in the literature.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Activation Interval Analysis
concepts.summary: Scoring each band of a feature's activation spectrum separately against the feature's overall hypothesis, to see how interpretability varies with activation strength.
concepts.explanation: Instead of asking whether a feature is interpretable, this asks whether a particular range of its activations is consistent with the hypothesis suggested by its full spectrum. The finding is that higher-activating intervals are more consistent with the interpretations than lower-activating ones. Two patterns appear: many features are consistent across the entire spectrum, while some are consistent across the top roughly 60% and then become rapidly less interpretable as activations shrink. The paper does not treat this as harmless — it says it is possible this is a sign the features are not quite right.

concepts.name: Features At A Slight Angle
concepts.summary: The paper's suggested explanation for the drop-off in low-interval interpretability: a learned direction slightly off from the true feature direction.
concepts.explanation: If a learned feature is at a slight angle to the feature the model actually uses, then near the top of the spectrum the two agree well, but further down the mismatch dominates and the feature's behavior stops matching the interpretation. The paper offers this as a possibility rather than a demonstration. It sits alongside the earlier [[weak-activation-hypotheses|three hypotheses for weak activations]] and points at the same open question: whether the dictionary has recovered the [[true-features]] or something close to them.

concepts.name: Feature-Proxy Correlation
concepts.summary: The Pearson correlation between a feature's activations and its computational proxy, used as a single number combining sensitivity and specificity.
concepts.explanation: The paper reports correlations of 0.74 for Arabic (proxy thresholded at zero, over 40 million tokens), 0.8 for DNA (binarized proxy), 0.55 for Hebrew, and 0.38 for base64. It describes correlation as a joint measure of sensitivity and specificity that takes magnitude into account, and calls 0.74 substantial. The lower numbers are attributed to proxy defects rather than feature impurity: the [[base64-proxy]] is too broad, and the Hebrew shortfall is partly a complementary feature. That attribution rests on inspection of disagreeing examples rather than an independent measurement.

concepts.name: Features are more universal than neurons
concepts.summary: Matching features across the two models gives a median activation correlation of 0.72; matching neurons across the same two transformers gives 0.46.
concepts.explanation: The neuron comparison is the control that makes the feature number mean something. Running the same closest-match procedure on the transformers' 512 neurons yields substantially less similarity. The paper states the conclusion in the summary as: sparse autoencoders applied to different models produce features more similar to one another than they are to their own model's neurons.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Expected Value Plot
concepts.summary: An activation histogram weighted by activation magnitude, so that the picture reflects how much effect a feature actually has rather than how many tokens it touches.
concepts.explanation: Borrowed from Cammarata et al.'s work on curve detectors, the expected value plot re-weights the distribution of feature activations by the activation level itself. This addresses the problem that a feature may fire weakly and imprecisely on many tokens and strongly and precisely on a few: an unweighted histogram overstates the weak, impure tail. For A/1/3450 the plot shows that most of the total activation magnitude comes from dataset examples that are in Arabic script. The paper returns to this plot in section 4.1.5 to argue that low-interval activations being less interpretable does not much damage the overall claim.

citedFrom.refText: Cammarata, Nick and Goh, Gabriel and Carter, Shan and Schubert, Ludwig and Petrov, Michael and Olah, Chris (2020). Curve Detectors. Distill
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The expected value plot is defined and motivated there; this paper uses the tool without redefining how it is constructed.

concepts.name: Feature Activation Distribution Broken Down by Proxy
concepts.summary: A histogram of a feature's activations with each bar colored by whether the proxy fires, used as the paper's basic specificity picture.
concepts.explanation: The paper's standard specificity display bins tokens by [[feature-activation]] level and colors each bin by proxy score, so the reader can see the proxy-positive fraction change with activation strength. For the Arabic feature that fraction goes from 25% at the weakest activations to 98% above activation 5. Alongside the histogram, the paper shows random dataset examples drawn from each activation level, so the reader can check the coloring against actual text rather than trusting the proxy.

concepts.name: Large Activations Matter Most
concepts.summary: The argument that getting the interpretation of strong activations right matters more than getting weak ones right, because strong activations move the logits more.
concepts.explanation: For the one-layer transformer studied here, the paper says the case is strong: features have a linear effect on the logits, modulo rescaling by layer norm, so a larger activation has a larger effect. For larger models the paper hedges explicitly — the claim then rests on conjectures and heuristic arguments about the abundance of linear pathways and about features being linear at each layer, and it must hold for sufficiently small activations by continuity, but there is no watertight argument. This is the load-bearing assumption behind treating impure weak activations as a secondary problem, and it is one of the places the paper's evidence is thinner than the claim it supports.

concepts.name: Three Hypotheses for Weak Activations
concepts.summary: The paper's three candidate explanations for why a feature's low activations look less pure than its high ones: the proxy is imperfect, the model is imperfect, or the autoencoder is imperfect.
concepts.explanation: The upper part of A/1/3450's spectrum is clearly specific to Arabic script; the lower part is muddier, and the paper offers three explanations without deciding between them. The proxy may be wrong; the model may be genuinely uncertain but calibrated; or the autoencoder may be too narrow to hold all the [[true-features]], so unrecovered features leak in as weak activations across many learned ones. The paper does not resolve which applies, and instead argues that it matters less than it might because [[large-activations-dominate]] the effect on model outputs.

concepts.name: Noise injection
concepts.summary: Adding noise during training as a separate route to sparse, interpretable representations.
concepts.explanation: Cited as earlier evidence that noise injection can increase neuron interpretability independently of an explicit sparsity penalty. The paper raises it as an untried alternative or complement to the L1 term.

citedFrom.refText: Bricken, Trenton and Schaeffer, Rylan and Olshausen, Bruno and Kreiman, Gabriel. Emergence of Sparse Representations from Noise.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The mechanism by which noise produces sparse representations is not described here at all.

concepts.name: Complementary Arabic Features
concepts.summary: The other features that fire in Arabic contexts and fill the gaps in A/1/3450's sensitivity.
concepts.explanation: A/1/3450 fails to fire on the very common prefix "ال" (the Arabic definite article), and in exactly those places A/1/3134 fires instead. Other features including A/1/1466 and A/1/3399 also contribute to representing Arabic script. The division is sometimes mechanical: when an Arabic character is split into two tokens, A/1/3450 fires on the final token of the character while A/1/3399 fires on the first. The paper presents an alternative visualization showing all features active on a snippet of Arabic text to make this collaboration visible.

concepts.name: Split Unicode Characters in Tokenization
concepts.summary: Non-Latin Unicode characters are often encoded as several byte tokens, which shapes where script features fire and which tokens their logit weights promote.
concepts.explanation: The tokenizer splits Unicode characters outside the Latin script into multiple byte tokens: ث (U+062B) becomes \xd8 followed by \xab. This matters for reading the activation visualizations, because A/1/3450 typically fires only on the last token of such a character while A/1/3399 fires on the first. It also matters for logit weights: \xd8 and \xd9 lead most basic Arabic characters and \xd7 leads most basic Hebrew characters, so those byte tokens appear prominently among the tokens a script feature makes more likely. The paper also flags this as extra difficulty for a very weak one-layer model trying to recognize what language it is reading.

concepts.name: Inducing activation sparsity during training
concepts.summary: Training the subject model itself to have few active neurons, in the hope that each neuron would then carry one feature.
concepts.explanation: The authors pushed this to the limit, including models with 1-hot activations where exactly one neuron fires at a time. This does eliminate superposition by construction — with one active neuron there is no linear combination to hide features in. But interpretable neurons did not follow. The argument they give generalizes: even in the 1-hot limit you can consider the single firing neuron and the cases where it fires, and it can still be advantageous for that neuron to be polysemantic.

concepts.name: Engineering monosemanticity in toy models
concepts.summary: Prior work finding multiple equal-loss minima in MLPs trained on a compressed sensing task, some polysemantic and some monosemantic.
concepts.explanation: Cited twice. It suggested that training interventions could steer models toward the more monosemantic minimum, which was one reason to hope for the architectural approach. The paper reports that subsequent investigation on more realistic tasks suggested the equal-loss property was specific to the chosen task, which is part of why the hope did not survive.

citedFrom.refText: Jermyn, Adam S and Schiefer, Nicholas and Hubinger, Evan. Engineering monosemanticity in toy models. arXiv:2211.09169
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The equal-loss-minima result and the task it depends on are the substance of the argument being cited and rebutted.

concepts.name: Why MSE models differ from language models
concepts.summary: Under mean squared error, polysemantic and monosemantic representations can reach the same loss, and for some feature importance curves the monosemantic solution is preferred — but language models are not trained with MSE.
concepts.explanation: This is the scope limit on the paper's negative result. Prior work on toy models found equal-loss minima under MSE, some strongly polysemantic and some strongly monosemantic, suggesting training interventions could steer toward the monosemantic ones; other work found MSE models can actively prefer monosemanticity for certain feature importance curves. The paper accepts these results and points out they do not transfer, because language models are trained on cross-entropy. The corollary is favorable: the [[sparse-autoencoder]] *is* trained with MSE, so its own sparsity penalty can inhibit superposition inside the dictionary.

concepts.name: Polysemanticity without superposition
concepts.summary: The finding that individual neurons can be polysemantic even when superposition has been ruled out, because ambiguous representations can achieve lower loss than unambiguous ones.
concepts.explanation: This is the result that closes off the architectural route. In many cases a model achieves lower loss by representing several features ambiguously in one neuron than by representing a single feature cleanly and ignoring the rest. Ignoring features is costly; representing them badly is cheaper than not representing them at all. The authors conclude that models trained on cross-entropy loss will generally prefer to represent more features polysemantically than fewer '[[true-features]]' monosemantically, even where sparsity constraints make superposition impossible.

concepts.name: SoLU activation
concepts.summary: An activation function proposed in earlier work to make more transformer neurons interpretable by encouraging features to align with the neuron basis.
concepts.explanation: SoLU is the authors' own earlier architectural attempt, and Section 6.2 gives its verdict: it appears to make some neurons more interpretable at the cost of making others even less interpretable than before. That pattern — a disentangling intervention causing the remaining features to entangle more strongly — is presented as characteristic of the difference between disentanglement and superposition. SoLU also matters positively in Section 5.3.2: base64, hexadecimal, and all-caps neurons found in SoLU models reappear as features here, which is the paper's strongest evidence for universality across architectures.

citedFrom.refText: Elhage, Nelson et al. (2022). Softmax Linear Units. Transformer Circuits Thread
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The activation function, the interpretability gains and losses it produces, and the specific neurons (base64, hex, all-caps, context and token-in-context neurons) that this paper matches its features against are all defined there.

concepts.name: Superposition all the way down
concepts.summary: The worry that the learned dictionary might itself use superposition, which the paper argues its MSE-plus-sparsity objective avoids.
concepts.explanation: If the decomposition tool suffered the same problem as the thing being decomposed, the features would be no better a unit of analysis than the neurons. The paper's argument that this does not happen rests on the loss function: [[dictionary-learning]] is trained with MSE reconstruction rather than cross-entropy, and under MSE the sparsity pressure can inhibit superposition forming rather than encouraging it. This is stated as a reason for confidence, not demonstrated.

concepts.name: The sharper-predictions argument
concepts.summary: The reason to think local codes are real: a compositional code forces the logits for 'the in Physics' to be a sum of two generic contributions, while a dedicated feature can be more specific.
concepts.explanation: If 'the' and Physics context were represented independently, the model's output would have to be 'upweight tokens which come after the' plus 'upweight tokens which occur in Physics'. A dedicated 'the in Physics' feature can instead predict exactly the noun phrases that follow 'the' in physics writing. The paper argues the model might want predictions sharper than the sum allows, and that only a [[local-code]] makes that possible. The [[feature-splitting]] results support this: split features have visibly more specific top logits than their parents.

concepts.name: Attribution vector
concepts.summary: For each sampled datapoint, the product of a feature's activation there and its logit weight on the token that actually came next.
concepts.explanation: If feature $i$ has logit weights $v_{ik}$ over the vocabulary, then at token $t_j$ the attribution score is $f_i(t_j)\,v_{i t_{j+1}}$, and the attribution vector stacks these scores over a random sample of datapoints. This approximates the classic gradient-times-activation attribution, differing in that it ignores the denominators of the softmax and the layer norm. It is the cheap substitute for computing a full vector of ablation effects for every feature on every datapoint, which the authors say would be computationally expensive.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Cross-Context Shuffling
concepts.summary: Activations are subsampled at 250 tokens per context and shuffled so that a training batch draws from many different contexts.
concepts.explanation: Tokens within a single context are highly correlated, so a batch made of consecutive tokens would be redundant and would present the autoencoder with a narrow slice of the activation distribution. Taking only 250 tokens from each of 40 million contexts and shuffling across contexts breaks that correlation. The paper separately lists dataset redundancy — too many tokens per context, or repeated epochs — as a cause of [[dead-neurons]], which is the failure this subsampling guards against.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Dataset and Basic Training

concepts.name: Sampling Without Replacement
concepts.summary: Each activation vector is seen at most once during autoencoder training. The paper says not repeating data is important for optimal results.
concepts.explanation: Because the collected dataset is larger than the number of vectors consumed — just over 8 billion used out of 10 billion — training can proceed for its full 1 million steps without ever revisiting a datapoint. The paper states plainly that sampling without replacement matters, and elsewhere lists repeated epochs over the same dataset among the causes of [[dead-neurons]]. It reports the finding without an accompanying ablation.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Dataset and Basic Training

concepts.name: Activation Prediction and Spearman Scoring
concepts.summary: Claude predicts activations for 60 nine-token examples from the explanation alone; the score is the Spearman correlation between predicted and true activations.
concepts.explanation: For each feature the model predicts activations on 60 dataset examples of nine tokens each, giving 540 predictions per feature, scored by Spearman correlation. The 60 comprise six from the top interval, two from each of the other twelve, ten completely random, and twenty top-activating tokens shown out of context; the examples are shuffled, and logits and interval labels are stripped. The paper notes that scoring on completely random sequences alone would be the most principled choice, but half the examples are drawn across intervals to get a more accurate correlation. For computational efficiency Claude scores all sixty examples in one shot, though the paper says that ideally each would be its own prompt. The appendix reports Pearson correlations too, with almost identical distributions and conclusions.

concepts.name: Quantizing Activations to 0–9
concepts.summary: Activations are rounded to integers 0 through 9 before being shown to or predicted by the language model.
concepts.explanation: Following Bills et al., all activations in the automated pipeline are quantized to integers between 0 and 9 inclusive. This makes the prediction task a small discrete output the model can produce token by token, and makes the demonstrations legible. It also means the automated scores are insensitive to fine differences in magnitude, which is part of why Spearman rather than exact-value agreement is the natural score.

citedFrom.refText: Bills, Steven et al. (2023). Language models can explain neurons in language models.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The 0–9 quantization convention originates there.

concepts.name: Automated Interpretability on Logit Weights
concepts.summary: Asking Claude, from the feature's explanation alone, whether an unseen high-logit token is one the feature should predict; features score 74% versus 58% for neurons against a 50% chance baseline.
concepts.explanation: Reusing the explanation generated for the activation task, the model is shown 100 logit tokens — 50 random and 50 drawn from the 10th to 60th largest positive logits, with the top 10 held out because they went into the explanation — and gives a binary label for each on whether that token would plausibly follow when the feature fires. Chance is 50%. The main text reports a 74% average across features against 58% across neurons; the appendix gives medians of 0.74 for A/1 features, 0.53 for neurons and 0.5 for the [[randomized-transformer]]. Failures counted in the figure are cases where Claude did not reply in the format needed for scoring. This is the automated version of the logit cross-check the individual case studies do by eye.

concepts.name: Constant Predictions Score Zero
concepts.summary: When Claude predicts the same value for everything — usually all zeros — no correlation exists, and the paper assigns a score of zero.
concepts.explanation: A correlation is undefined if one series has no variance. The paper handles this by assigning such cases a score of zero, and notes that this explains a visible uptick at zero in the score distributions. This convention interacts badly with [[importance-scoring]], where always predicting zero becomes a way to score well rather than a failure.

concepts.name: Explanation Generation Setup
concepts.summary: The exact prompt composition used to get a feature explanation out of Claude 2: 49 examples of specified kinds, plus logits, interval labels, and eight worked demonstrations.
concepts.explanation: Claude 2 is given ten examples from the top [[activation-interval]], two from each of the other twelve intervals, five completely random examples, and ten examples where the feature's top activating tokens appear in different contexts — 49 in total. It also sees the feature's top and bottom logits and a label saying which interval each example came from. Eight human demonstrations on held-out features, including chain-of-thought reasoning, are included. The model is asked to be succinct and not to name specific tokens it activates for. Features with fewer than 49 available examples occur when repeated examples are removed, and any feature left with fewer than 20 examples total is dropped.

concepts.name: Explanation Lengths Caveat
concepts.summary: Claude sometimes fails to wrap its explanation in answer tags, so the full chain of thought is used instead — a null result, since it does not change scores.
concepts.explanation: When the model does not close its explanation in <answer></answer> tags, the whole chain of thought gets used as the explanation. That text is much longer and can leak specific tokens the feature fires for, which would be an unfair advantage. Plotting explanation character counts shows these cases as a second mode to the right. The paper reports that this happens infrequently and, importantly for the comparison, most often for neurons (19%) rather than features (13%), with the [[randomized-transformer]] in between (15%) — and that splitting performance by long versus short explanations does not give significantly different scores. So the artifact exists but does not favor the paper's conclusion.

concepts.name: Importance Scoring
concepts.summary: A reweighting that corrects for the non-random sampling of scored examples — and which, in this setting, mostly collapses feature scores toward zero.
concepts.explanation: Because the scored examples are deliberately drawn from across activation intervals rather than at random, the score does not reflect performance on the real data distribution. Importance scoring corrects this: tokens from random examples get weight 1, and examples from each feature interval get weight equal to feature_density times interval_probability, where feature_density is how often the feature fires over a large portion of the dataset and interval_probability is the probability of that interval under the distribution of non-zero activations. Top-activating-tokens-out-of-context examples inherit the top interval's weighting. These weights are then used in the Spearman correlation. The paper presents this as the principled correction and then argues it fails in practice.

concepts.name: No Leakage of Activation Information
concepts.summary: The design constraint that nothing about a feature's activation pattern reaches the prediction step except through the written explanation.
concepts.explanation: The paper states this explicitly: when predicting new activations, the model cannot see any true activations of that feature, and the examples used to generate the explanation are kept separate from those used to test prediction. This is what makes the score a measure of the explanation's quality rather than of pattern-matching. It also constrains the logit task, where the top 10 logits used to generate the original explanation are held out of the 100 logits the model is later asked to judge.

concepts.name: Base64 Digit Feature and the BPE Exploit
concepts.summary: A companion feature that fires on single digits inside base64 contexts, exploiting a property of the BPE tokenizer to make a better prediction.
concepts.explanation: A/1/2357 does not fire on some digits inside base64 strings — the 2, 4, 7 and 9 visible in the paper's figure. One of two other base64-context features fires on single digits instead. The paper says this feature exploits a property of the byte-pair-encoding tokenizer to make a better prediction, and defers the details to a later section. It is another instance of the pattern that gaps in one feature's coverage are filled by a sibling.

concepts.name: Hexadecimal Feature (A/1/3817)
concepts.summary: A separate feature for hexadecimal strings, which the base64 proxy wrongly counts as base64.
concepts.explanation: Strings drawn from [0-9A-F] activate the [[base64-proxy]], since they are quite different from the overall data distribution and fall inside the base64 character class. But they are predicted by their own feature, A/1/3817, not by A/1/2357. The paper cites this as the main reason the base64 proxy correlation is only 0.38 — the proxy is broader than the feature, not the other way around.

concepts.name: The Earlier Base64 Neuron
concepts.summary: A base64 neuron previously found in the SoLU paper, which the authors take as a hint that base64 might be universal across architectures and datasets.
concepts.explanation: The paper says it is particularly interested in the [[base64-feature]] because a base64 neuron had already been discovered in its earlier Softmax Linear Units work. That model had a somewhat different dataset and a different architecture, so finding the same concept again suggests base64 may be a genuinely universal feature rather than an artifact of this setup. This is weaker evidence than the A-versus-B matching, since it is an observation about a different study rather than a controlled comparison.

citedFrom.refText: Elhage, Nelson et al. (2022). Softmax Linear Units. Transformer Circuits Thread
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The base64 neuron, the SoLU architecture, and the evaluation methodology this paper is reacting against are all described there.

concepts.name: Tokenization artifacts in features
concepts.summary: Some feature behavior reflects the tokenizer rather than the content — the digit base64 feature suppresses digits because consecutive digits would have been merged into one token.
concepts.explanation: If a single-digit token were followed by another digit, the tokenizer would have merged them: [Bq][8][9][mp] never occurs because it would be tokenized [Bq][89][mp]. So in a random base64 string, seeing a lone digit token is real evidence the next token is not a digit, and the feature correctly encodes that. The same effect drives the two-node automata for Unicode scripts, where characters are split into prefix and suffix tokens. The lesson the paper draws is that a feature can look strange until you account for the tokenizer.

concepts.name: NP-Hardness of Exact Recovery
concepts.summary: Compressed sensing in its exact form is NP-hard, which the paper turns into an argument about what method to use.
concepts.explanation: Finding the exactly sparsest coefficient vector consistent with an observation is NP-hard, so all practical [[dictionary-learning]] methods solve a relaxed version or search greedily. The paper draws an unusual conclusion from this: since the transformer itself certainly is not solving an NP-hard problem, a recovery method that is too strong might extract structure the model cannot itself use. That reasoning is what pushes it toward a method with roughly the same computational shape as the model's own MLP.

sections.title: Using Sparse Autoencoders To Find Good Decompositions

concepts.name: Arabic Script Proxy
concepts.summary: The per-token score $\log(P(s|\text{Arabic Script}) / P(s))$, built from the Arabic Unicode blocks.
concepts.explanation: Arabic, Farsi and Urdu all use the Arabic script, which occupies well-defined Unicode blocks, so membership is easy to compute. The proxy scores each token by how much more likely the string is under an Arabic-script hypothesis than under the dataset at large. It has known false negatives: characters common to many scripts, such as whitespace, punctuation, and newlines, fall outside the Arabic blocks and score low even inside Arabic text. Thresholded at zero, this proxy has a Pearson correlation of 0.74 with A/1/3450's activity over 40 million tokens.

concepts.name: Base64 Proxy
concepts.summary: A score modeling base64 strings as random sequences over [a-zA-Z0-9+/]; the paper judges it too broad.
concepts.explanation: The base64 proxy correlates with A/1/2357's activity at only 0.38, and the paper attributes most of that gap to the proxy rather than the feature. The character class [a-zA-Z0-9+/] also covers hexadecimal strings from [0-9A-F], which look very unlike the overall data distribution and so score highly on the proxy — but those are handled by a separate feature, A/1/3817. The paper's reading is that the proxy fires on things that are not base64, dragging the correlation down while the feature itself remains specific.

concepts.name: Character-Distribution Proxies
concepts.summary: For features about character sets like base64 or DNA, the conditional probability is modeled as a uniform draw over the allowed characters.
concepts.explanation: For base64 the paper assumes a random base64 string, assigning each of the 64 base64 characters probability $1/64$ and everything else $10^{-10}$, then takes the product over characters. DNA is modeled the same way as a random string over [ATCG] with probability 1/4 each. The tiny probability for disallowed characters is what makes the proxy sharply penalize any string that breaks the pattern. The paper notes it found this approach helpful for hexadecimal, binary and similar features too, though those are not used in the draft.

concepts.name: DNA Proxy
concepts.summary: A score for "is a DNA sequence", modeling DNA as random strings over [ATCG] and evaluated on groups of at least two tokens.
concepts.explanation: Some single vocabulary tokens, such as CAT, occur both in nucleotide sequences and in ordinary text, so the proxy is always evaluated over groups of at least two tokens. Its log-probabilities turn out to be strongly bimodal, so the paper binarizes it on the sign of the score. The binarized proxy has a Pearson correlation of 0.8 with A/1/2937's activations. The paper notes the proxy is less sensitive to DNA than the feature is, missing strings that contain punctuation, spaces, or missing bases.

concepts.name: Hebrew Script Proxy
concepts.summary: A Unicode-block-based score for Hebrew text, correlating 0.55 with A/1/416.
concepts.explanation: As with Arabic, Hebrew text is easy to identify computationally from its Unicode blocks. The Pearson correlation of this proxy with A/1/416 is 0.55, lower than the Arabic case. The paper attributes some of the shortfall in sensitivity to a complementary feature, A/1/1016, which fires on \xd7 and predicts the bytes that complete Hebrew characters' codepoints. It also notes that strong activations sometimes score low on the proxy because they land on whitespace or punctuation from other Unicode blocks.

concepts.name: Log-Likelihood Ratio Form
concepts.summary: Proxies take the form $\log(P(s|\text{hypothesis})/P(s))$ — how much more likely the string is under the feature's hypothesis than under the general distribution.
concepts.explanation: Using a ratio rather than the raw conditional probability controls for strings being intrinsically common or rare: a string that is likely under the hypothesis but also likely everywhere is not evidence for the feature. The paper's stated reason for the log form is that features interact linearly with the logits, so they should be incentivized to track log-likelihoods — meaning the proxy is on the same scale as whatever the feature is plausibly computing. This is an intuition about what a feature ought to represent, offered as justification for the choice of proxy rather than derived.

concepts.name: Maximizing Over Prefixes
concepts.summary: The proxy is evaluated over multiple prefixes ending at the token in question, and the maximum is taken.
concepts.explanation: A feature's activation at a token can depend on what came before — the paper's example is that an Arabic feature could fire more strongly toward the end of a long Arabic string. A proxy computed on the single token alone would miss this, and one computed on a fixed-length window would be arbitrary. The paper instead computes the log-likelihood ratio over different prefixes leading up to and including the final token and takes the maximum. This choice also does work in the script proxies, where a prefix containing any non-script character is assigned a near-zero conditional probability — maximizing over prefixes lets a shorter, purely-Arabic suffix still score high.

concepts.name: Proxy Binarization
concepts.summary: Reducing a proxy's continuous log-probability to a yes/no value based on its sign, done when the proxy's distribution is strongly bimodal.
concepts.explanation: For DNA the log-probabilities produced by the proxy come out strongly bimodal — strings are clearly nucleotide sequences or clearly not — so the paper collapses the score to a binary value on its sign before correlating it with feature activations. The Arabic proxy is similarly thresholded at zero when computing its correlation with A/1/3450. Binarizing loses magnitude information, but for a bimodal score there is little magnitude information to lose.

concepts.name: Where the Proxies Fail
concepts.summary: The paper's catalog of cases where feature and proxy disagree because the proxy is wrong, not the feature.
concepts.explanation: Across the case studies the paper repeatedly finds the proxy at fault rather than the feature. Arabic and Hebrew proxies miss whitespace, punctuation and newlines that sit outside the target Unicode blocks even when embedded in target-script text. The [[dna-proxy]] fails on triplets separated by spaces, such as "TGG AGT", and on the prefix 5'- where the feature fires productively because DNA is about to follow. The [[base64-proxy]] is too broad, also firing on hexadecimal. The paper reports that in all but two disagreements for DNA, the feature was right and the proxy was wrong — which means the reported correlations are lower bounds on how well the features track their contexts.

concepts.name: Script Proxies via Bayes' Rule
concepts.summary: For features about writing systems, $P(s|\text{script})$ is obtained by inverting an easy-to-compute $P(\text{script}|s)$.
concepts.explanation: Directly modeling the distribution of Arabic text is hard, but detecting whether a string is Arabic is easy, so the paper uses $P(s|\text{Arabic}) = P(\text{Arabic}|s) \cdot P(s) / P(\text{Arabic})$. $P(s)$ comes from the unigram model. $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ is 1 if the string consists entirely of Arabic characters and $10^{-10}$ otherwise. $P(\text{Arabic})$ is estimated by applying the same character heuristic to a random sample of the dataset. The same construction is used for other scripts with distinctive Unicode blocks.

concepts.name: Estimating $P(s)$ with a Unigram Model
concepts.summary: The denominator of every proxy is computed as the product of independent per-token unigram probabilities.
concepts.explanation: The paper estimates a string's probability under the full empirical distribution as $P(s) = \prod_{t \in s} p(t)$, using the unigram distribution over tokens. This ignores all dependency between tokens, so it will systematically overestimate the surprise of ordinary fluent text. The paper does not correct for this; it is the simplest available baseline for 'how likely is this string in general'.

concepts.name: De Facto Dead Neurons
concepts.summary: Ultralow density neurons that fire so rarely they are effectively dead, but do not register as dead by a zero-activity check.
concepts.explanation: The paper notes a nuance: with more training steps, networks kill off more ultralow-density neurons, meaning that at fewer steps such neurons exist in a state where they fire occasionally but contribute nothing useful. Counting only strictly [[dead-neurons]] therefore understates the waste. The paper uses this to argue for tracking the size of the [[high-density-cluster]] rather than the dead neuron count, since the former is not fooled by neurons that are dead in practice.

concepts.name: Unit-Norm Dictionary Columns
concepts.summary: The columns of $W_d$ are constrained to have L2 norm 1, so that the L1 penalty cannot be gamed by shrinking directions.
concepts.explanation: Without a norm constraint, the model could drive the L1 penalty down by making feature activations tiny and dictionary vectors correspondingly long, leaving the reconstruction unchanged while the penalty vanishes. Fixing each column to unit norm removes that degree of freedom and makes activation magnitudes comparable across features. The constraint has a cost: it interacts badly with a naive optimizer implementation, which the paper addresses separately.

concepts.name: Fitting Activations Only
concepts.summary: The decomposition is fit to the MLP activations alone, ignoring what those activations do to the model's output — which leaves downstream effects available as a check.
concepts.explanation: Nothing in the training objective mentions logits, loss, or any downstream consequence of a [[feature-direction]] $\mathbf{d}_i$. The paper flags this as deliberate: because downstream effects were never optimized for, later analyses that show a feature has a coherent effect on the output are evidence the feature is real and not an artifact of the fitting procedure. The same logic underlies feature ablations, which measure the output-side consequences of directions found purely on the input side.

sections.title: Using Sparse Autoencoders To Find Good Decompositions

concepts.name: Classical Dictionary Learning Algorithms
concepts.summary: Established iterative methods such as Method of Optimal Directions and K-SVD. The paper tried several and set them aside.
concepts.explanation: There is a mature literature of [[dictionary-learning]] algorithms that alternate between solving for sparse codes and updating the dictionary, typically via a relaxed optimization or a greedy search. The paper says it tried several of these classic methods before settling on a [[sparse-autoencoder]] instead. It gives two reasons: the autoencoder scales to very large datasets, and the iterative methods risk being 'too strong'. The paper does not report comparative results for the classical methods it tried.

citedFrom.refText: Aharon, Michal and Elad, Michael and Bruckstein, Alfred (2006). K-SVD: An algorithm for designing overcomplete dictionaries for sparse representation. IEEE Transactions on signal processing
citedFrom.whyNeeded: K-SVD and Method of Optimal Directions are named as the alternatives that were tried and rejected; how they work is only in the cited papers.

sections.title: Using Sparse Autoencoders To Find Good Decompositions

concepts.name: Compressed Sensing
concepts.summary: The problem of recovering a sparse high-dimensional vector from a low-dimensional linear measurement of it. The paper names this as the hard inner problem inside dictionary learning.
concepts.explanation: Even if you were handed the true feature directions $\mathbf{d}_i$, you would still have to compute the activations $f_i(\mathbf{x})$ for each datapoint — that is, invert a very rectangular matrix and get a high-dimensional vector out of a low-dimensional projection. On its face this is impossible; the only thing that makes it possible is that the answer is known to be sparse. The paper calls this the famous and well-studied problem of compressed sensing. Its point is that sparse structure can be stored in a lower-dimensional space, but getting it back out is genuinely hard work, not bookkeeping.

sections.title: Using Sparse Autoencoders To Find Good Decompositions

concepts.name: Parallel sparse autoencoder investigation
concepts.summary: An independent line of interim reports and a manuscript investigating the same sparse autoencoder approach, prompted by Toy Models.
concepts.explanation: The paper credits Sharkey et al. for focusing on [[dictionary-learning]] and specifically the [[sparse-autoencoder]] while the authors were exploring it as only one of several approaches. That work was partly replicated by Cunningham & Smith and by Huben; Smith then found features in one MLP layer of a six-layer model and later in its residual stream; Cunningham applied [[automated-interpretability]] to those features and found them substantially more interpretable than neurons. The line culminates in the Cunningham et al. manuscript, which the authors cite as evidence the approach can work on somewhat larger models.

citedFrom.refText: Cunningham, Hoagy and Ewart, Aidan and Smith, Logan and Huben, Robert and Sharkey, Lee. Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Model Directions. arXiv:2309.08600
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The main external evidence cited for the approach scaling beyond one-layer models; the models, metrics and scale used there matter to that claim.

concepts.name: Mean max cosine similarity (MMCS)
concepts.summary: A measure of how well features from two separately trained dictionaries match up, reported elsewhere as bimodal; the paper suspects density bimodality explains it.
concepts.explanation: Huben reported that [[sparse-autoencoder]] features are bimodal under a cross-dictionary comparison, where each feature in one dictionary is matched to its closest counterpart in another by cosine similarity and the resulting similarities are averaged. The paper suggests in an aside that the bimodality in [[feature-density]] it observes might partially explain that finding — ultralow density features would not be expected to match across dictionaries, so a mixture of two feature populations would produce two modes in the similarity distribution. This is offered as a suspicion, not a result.

citedFrom.refText: Lee Sharkey and Dan Braun and Beren Millidge (2022). [Interim research report] Taking features out of superposition with sparse autoencoders.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: MMCS is defined and used there; this paper names it without giving the definition.

concepts.name: Overcompleteness
concepts.summary: Having more dictionary directions than the dimension of the space they live in. The paper insists this is what separates its setting from ordinary disentanglement work.
concepts.explanation: An overcomplete dictionary has $m \geq n$ elements in an $n$-dimensional space, so the directions cannot be linearly independent and the decomposition is not unique on its face. The paper argues this apparently small change is what makes the setting hard and interesting: with an ordinary basis you could just solve for the coefficients, whereas here you are trying to pin down a high-dimensional coefficient vector from a low-dimensional observation. It is also the whole point, since the premise is that the MLP layer packs more features into its activations than it has neurons. The paper says it is 'kind of miraculous' that recovery works at all.

concepts.name: Earlier dictionary learning on embeddings
concepts.summary: A body of pre-transformer work applying sparse coding, sparse autoencoders, dictionary learning and topic-model methods to word embeddings.
concepts.explanation: Related Work lists Faruqui et al. and Arora et al. finding linear structure in word embeddings via sparse coding, Subramanian et al. finding linear factors with a [[sparse-autoencoder]], Zhang et al. using [[dictionary-learning]] methods, and Panigrahi et al. approaching the same problem with Latent Dirichlet Allocation. The paper cites these to place its own method in a tradition rather than to import specific results.

concepts.name: Sparse autoencoder
concepts.summary: A one-hidden-layer autoencoder with a wide ReLU hidden layer and an L1 penalty on that layer, trained to reconstruct MLP activations. Its hidden units are the learned features and its decoder columns are the feature directions.
concepts.explanation: The paper's [[dictionary-learning]] approximation is a small MLP trained as an autoencoder: input weights act as the encoder, output weights as the decoder, and the hidden layer is much wider than the input. Formally, with $W_e \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$, $W_d \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m}$ and biases $\mathbf{b}_e, \mathbf{b}_d$, the forward pass is $\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_d$, $\mathbf{f} = \text{ReLU}(W_e\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{b}_e)$, $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = W_d\mathbf{f} + \mathbf{b}_d$. The hidden activations $\mathbf{f}$ are the learned feature activations and the columns of $W_d$ are the dictionary vectors. The paper picks this over classical dictionary learning because it scales to billions of datapoints and because its architecture resembles the MLP layers it is decomposing.

citedFrom.refText: Lee Sharkey and Dan Braun and Beren Millidge (2022). [Interim research report] Taking features out of superposition with sparse autoencoders.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The paper describes its autoencoder as 'similar to Sharkey, et al.' — the prior version of this method and how it differs is in that report.

sections.title: Using Sparse Autoencoders To Find Good Decompositions
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: Sparsity of Natural Latent Variables
concepts.summary: The long-standing hypothesis that the underlying variables generating natural data are mostly inactive at any moment. The paper uses it to justify asking for a sparse decomposition.
concepts.explanation: The paper invokes a hypothesis going back to sparse coding work in vision: most latent variables describing the world are off most of the time, so any given input reflects only a handful of them. It concedes that our understanding of what features actually exist in language models is limited, but says the examples available so far are suggestive of highly sparse variables. This is a motivating prior, not a measurement — the paper offers it as the reason to prefer sparse decompositions rather than as evidence that they are correct.

citedFrom.refText: Olshausen, Bruno A and Field, David J (1997). Sparse coding with an overcomplete basis set: A strategy employed by V1?. Vision research
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The argument for why sparseness is the right prior lives in that paper's "Why Sparseness?" section, which this paper points at directly.

sections.title: Using Sparse Autoencoders To Find Good Decompositions

concepts.name: A deliberately weak dictionary learning algorithm
concepts.summary: The worry that a sufficiently sophisticated decomposition method could recover structure from the activations that the model itself has no way to read out.
concepts.explanation: If the goal is to describe how the model works, a method that extracts features the model cannot access would be finding structure in the data rather than in the computation. The paper argues that a [[sparse-autoencoder]] is a reasonable guard against this, because its architecture — a linear map followed by ReLU — is very close to the MLP layers of the language model, and so should be about as powerful at reading features out of superposition. This is an argument from architectural similarity, not a proof, and the paper presents it as intuition.

sections.title: Using Sparse Autoencoders To Find Good Decompositions

concepts.name: Why disentangling can make things worse
concepts.summary: The paper's claim that pushing a model to disentangle its dimensions typically hurts performance, and that models respond by entangling some features more strongly.
concepts.explanation: The reasoning: success at disentanglement would require the model to throw away many features, since it has more features than dimensions. So the pressure gets absorbed elsewhere. The paper cites two cases where this was observed in different contexts — concept bottleneck models, and its own SoLU work where some neurons became more interpretable while others became less. This is offered as the key distinction between the two problems, not just a difference of emphasis.

concepts.name: Factors of variation
concepts.summary: The conceptually distinct influences on the data that a disentangled representation is supposed to separate into independent dimensions.
concepts.explanation: The target object of disentanglement, analogous to features here but constrained in number to the dimensionality of the latent space. The difference in framing is what the paper's Section 6.2 argument turns on: if the model genuinely wants more factors than dimensions, insisting that dimensions be independent forces it to throw features away.

concepts.name: TopK activation
concepts.summary: Keeping only the k largest hidden activations and zeroing the rest, as a hard way to enforce sparsity.
concepts.explanation: Cited as an early disentanglement-by-sparsity method — a k-sparse autoencoder. It is the direct alternative to the L1 penalty this paper uses: TopK fixes the number of active units exactly, while an L1 penalty makes sparsity a soft, tunable pressure whose level varies per datapoint.

citedFrom.refText: Alireza Makhzani and Brendan J. Frey (2013). k-Sparse Autoencoders. CoRR
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The mechanism and training details of a k-sparse autoencoder are the natural comparison point for this paper's L1 approach and are not described here.

concepts.name: Feature Density
concepts.summary: The fraction of tokens on which a feature has a nonzero value; the paper's main quick proxy for autoencoder quality.
concepts.explanation: Every feature in the autoencoder fires on only a very small percentage of tokens, and the density is that percentage. The paper hypothesizes that language models contain many features spread across a distribution of densities, and that lower-density features are harder for the autoencoder to find because they appear less often in training — which is why it uses large training datasets. Two summary numbers are read off the density distribution: how many features were recovered, and the minimum density among recovered features. The paper says these track subjective autoencoder quality well enough to be useful for fast iteration, and describes them as anecdotal.

concepts.name: Feature Exploration Interface
concepts.summary: A published visualization covering every feature in every dictionary learning run, showing when a feature fires, what it does to the logits, and what happens when it is ablated.
concepts.explanation: Rather than printing everything, the paper hosts visualizations for A/1, A/0, the neurons, and the randomized model, and asks readers to check its claims there. Each shows a feature's activations across intervals with dataset examples, its logit weights, its ablation effects displayed as underlines, and its [[automated-interpretability]] score. Features can be sorted by 'random' for an unbiased sample, or by importance metrics such as max activation and max density. The paper leans on these for several claims it does not otherwise substantiate in text — notably that the randomized model's non-single-token features resist interpretation.

sections.title: Do features tell us about the model or the data?

concepts.name: The Information-Based Metric That Failed
concepts.summary: An attempt to score factorizations by the total information of autoencoder plus data. It did not correlate with what the paper cared about.
concepts.explanation: The idea was to call the best factorization the one minimizing the combined description length of the autoencoder and the data given it. The paper reports this total information did not generally track either subjective feature interpretability or activation sparsity: runs whose feature activations had average L0 norms in the hundreds but low reconstruction error could score better than runs with far sparser codes and worse reconstruction. This is reported as a negative result and the approach was dropped.

sections.title: How can we tell if the autoencoder is working?

concepts.name: Sparsity vs. Explained Behavior Tradeoff
concepts.summary: Plotting $L^0$ norm against reconstructed transformer NLL across runs gives a frontier the paper uses to choose the L1 coefficient.
concepts.explanation: Neither sparsity nor faithfulness is meaningful on its own — you can have either by giving up the other. Taken together they lay out a human-interpretable tradeoff: each line on the paper's plot is one [[l1-coefficient]] with autoencoder size varying along it, so the family of lines shows what you get by moving $\lambda$ versus by making the dictionary bigger. The lowest L1 coefficient is excluded from the plot to keep the scale reasonable. The paper uses this frontier to pick hyperparameters rather than any single scalar score.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

concepts.name: $L^0$ Norm
concepts.summary: The average number of features active on a token. This is the paper's direct measure of how sparse the decomposition actually is.
concepts.explanation: The L1 penalty is a stand-in for the thing you actually want to control: how many features are nonzero at once, which is the $L^0$ norm of $\mathbf{f}$. The paper reports it as an average over datapoints and says it generally targets values under 10 or 20, while admitting it knows no principled way to pick a target level of sparsity. It especially distrusts solutions where the $L^0$ norm is a significant fraction of the transformer's activation dimensionality — at that point the decomposition has stopped being sparse relative to the 512 neurons it is meant to be unpacking.

sections.title: How can we tell if the autoencoder is working?
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

concepts.name: Manual Inspection
concepts.summary: Looking at features and asking whether they seem interpretable. Slow and subjective, but the paper treats it as the ground truth the proxies stand in for.
concepts.explanation: The paper's stated goal is interpretable features, and it says quantitatively measuring interpretability is currently difficult and slow — which is why it uses proxy metrics when testing changes or optimizing hyperparameters. Manual inspection is what those proxies are proxies for. The paper also warns about reading it too confidently: at various points features that at first made no sense became understandable with deeper inspection.

sections.title: How can we tell if the autoencoder is working?
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

concepts.name: Toy Models as Ground Truth
concepts.summary: Small synthetic setups where the true features are known by construction, used to check that the autoencoder recovers what it should.
concepts.explanation: Because there is no way to verify recovered features against ground truth in a real transformer, the paper leaned on toy models where the underlying features were put there by hand. It says having these was crucial to its early progress, and several architectural choices — the [[pre-encoder-bias|pre-encoder bias]] in particular — were decided on toy problems rather than on the real autoencoder. The limitation is the obvious one: what works on a constructed toy distribution need not transfer.

citedFrom.refText: Elhage, Nelson et al. (2022). Toy Models of Superposition. Transformer Circuits Thread
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The toy models used as ground truth, and the bounce plots and superposition results they produce, are defined in that prior work.
