concepts.name: Feature direction
concepts.summary: The unit vector $\mathbf{d}_i$ in activation space along which feature $i$ writes when it fires; in the autoencoder these are the columns of the decoder weight matrix.
concepts.explanation: The direction says how the feature is written into the layer's activations, as opposed to the activation $f_i$ which says how strongly. Because directions are unit vectors, all magnitude information lives in $f_i$. Geometric relationships between directions carry meaning in this paper: conceptually similar features turn out to have small angles between their dictionary vectors, which is the basis of the UMAP clustering and of the [[feature-splitting]] story.

concepts.name: The linear-representation exchange
concepts.summary: An exchange in which one paper found an apparent counterexample to features-as-directions and a second resolved it by finding an alternative, linear interpretation.
concepts.explanation: Li et al. reported a sequence model whose learned world representation did not appear to be encoded in linear directions, which the paper describes as putting the hypothesis in jeopardy. Nanda et al. then found an alternative framing of the same representation under which the features *were* directions. The authors highlight the exchange as an update on whether the general picture of features as directions is correct, and treat it as strengthening rather than weakening the hypothesis.

citedFrom.refText: Nanda, Neel and Lee, Andrew and Wattenberg, Martin. Emergent Linear Representations in World Models of Self-Supervised Sequence Models. arXiv:2309.00941
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The resolution of the apparent counterexample is what the paper's confidence in features-as-directions partly rests on; the re-interpretation's details matter.

concepts.name: Vector arithmetic in word embeddings
concepts.summary: The classic observation that relationships between words correspond to consistent offsets between their embedding vectors.
concepts.explanation: Cited as early evidence that latent spaces have interpretable linear directions. The paper cites it with an explicit caveat — 'but see' a later paper questioning the interpretation — which is characteristic of how it treats this evidence base: suggestive rather than settled.

citedFrom.refText: Mikolov, Tomáš and Yih, Wen-tau and Zweig, Geoffrey (2013). Linguistic regularities in continuous space word representations. NAACL-HLT
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The original demonstration of linear structure in embeddings, one of the pillars of the linear representation hypothesis.

concepts.name: Are token-in-context features real?
concepts.summary: Whether the hundreds of 'the'-in-a-context features reflect the transformer's own local code, or an artifact of dictionary learning imposing one.
concepts.explanation: The paper states two hypotheses cleanly. Either the transformer uses a [[compositional-code]] and a quirk of the [[dictionary-learning]] scheme renders it as a local one — in which case a better scheme could recover the compositional features, and the L1 penalty may be pushing too far toward sparsity. Or the transformer genuinely uses a [[local-code]] at least in part, and dictionary learning is representing it correctly. The authors say they believe the second holds to some extent, while conceding the first is a live possibility. This is one of the paper's more explicit uncertainties about its own method.

concepts.name: Compositional code
concepts.summary: A representation where independent units combine to represent a conjunction — 'the' and 'Physics' active together.
concepts.explanation: More economical in units, and the arrangement one would intuitively expect. Its constraint is that downstream effects add: if token and context are independent features, the resulting logits must be the sum of their separate contributions. That additivity is exactly what the paper argues the model may not want.

concepts.name: Local code
concepts.summary: A representation with one dedicated unit per thing represented, including per combination of properties.
concepts.explanation: Sparse by construction — one unit active per represented item — which makes it the code an L1 penalty tends to favor. The paper's [[token-in-context-features|token-in-context features]] are local codes over token-context pairs. Its argument that this may be genuine rests on prediction sharpness: a dedicated unit for a pair can output whatever distribution it likes for that pair.

concepts.name: Excluding Anomalous Tokens
concepts.summary: Logit weights for extremely rare or never-used vocabulary elements are dropped from the plots.
concepts.explanation: The paper excludes weights corresponding to vocabulary elements that are extremely rare or never used in training, noting these are perhaps similar to the anomalous tokens such as "SolidGoldMagikarp" reported by Rumbelow and Watkins. Such tokens can have arbitrary unembedding directions because training never constrained them, so leaving them in would put meaningless outliers in every [[logit-weight-histogram]].

citedFrom.refText: Rumbelow, Jessica and Watkins, Matthew (2023). SolidGoldMagikarp (plus, prompt generation).
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The anomalous-token phenomenon and why untrained vocabulary entries behave strangely is described there, not here.

concepts.name: Direct path
concepts.summary: The route from token embedding straight to the unembedding, bypassing attention and the MLP.
concepts.explanation: Named in Section 5.3.1 as one of the things that may already have suppressed a token's logit before the MLP features contribute anything. It matters for reading logit weights: a feature's large negative weight on an already-impossible token has no effect on behavior, so logit weights overstate the practical significance of parts of the vocabulary. This is the reasoning that motivates the [[attribution-vector]].

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Linearizing Layer Norm
concepts.summary: Approximating layer norm as a fixed projection removing the mean plus a diagonal scaling matrix, so a feature's path to the logits stays linear.
concepts.explanation: Layer norm is not linear, which would break the path expansion. The paper approximates it by combining a projection that removes the mean with a diagonal matrix standing in for the scaling terms, and folds this into the [[logit-weight]] computation as the factors $\pi L$. The paper lists a poor layer norm approximation as one of three ways the logit weights could overestimate a feature's real influence, and says the subsequent ablation analysis, which confirms the logit weight effects, gives it confidence that this is not a problem in practice.

citedFrom.refText: Elhage, Nelson et al. (2021). A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits. Transformer Circuits Thread
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The paper points to Framework for the layer norm linearization it uses rather than restating it.

concepts.name: Ways Logit Weights Could Mislead
concepts.summary: Three stated ways the linear logit weight could overstate a feature's real influence on the model.
concepts.explanation: The paper lists them: the output weights might be small enough that, multiplied by realistic activations, they barely move the output; the feature might only fire in situations where other features already make those tokens extremely unlikely, so it has little net effect; and the [[layer-norm-linearization]] might be a poor approximation. The paper says that based on the subsequent ablation analysis, which confirms the [[logit-weight]] effects, it does not believe these issues arise in practice. That is the argument for why ablation is run at all rather than trusting the linear picture.

concepts.name: Median-Centering the Logit Weights
concepts.summary: Because softmax is shift-invariant, logit weights have no absolute scale; the paper shifts each feature's weights so its median is zero.
concepts.explanation: Adding a constant to every logit leaves the softmax output unchanged, so the raw logit weights for a feature are only meaningful up to a shift. The paper fixes this by subtracting each feature's median [[logit-weight]], making the bulk mode sit at zero. This is what makes the "second mode on the far right" reading possible: it is a mode of tokens promoted relative to the typical token, not in any absolute sense.

concepts.name: The Second Mode in Logit Weights
concepts.summary: The recurring finding that a feature's logit weight histogram has a large mode at zero plus a small, far-right mode of tokens specific to the feature's context.
concepts.explanation: For every case study the paper finds this shape. For Arabic the second mode is Arabic characters and the leading byte tokens \xd8 and \xd9; for DNA it is nucleotide combinations like AGT and GCC; for Hebrew it is Hebrew characters and \xd7; for base64 it is base64-specific tokens. The matched features in run B show the same structure, and in the two-dimensional scatter of A against B logit weights the context tokens cluster together in one corner. The base64 case is the one exception to the clean separation, transitioning more continuously because many English-letter tokens have some genuine base64 probability.

concepts.name: MLP output weights
concepts.summary: The matrix $W_{down}$ that maps MLP activations back into the residual stream.
concepts.explanation: The second weight matrix of the MLP block, taking the 512 post-ReLU activations back down into the 128-dimensional residual stream. A [[feature-direction]] is multiplied through it first when computing logit weights, since that is how the feature's contribution reaches the rest of the model.

concepts.name: Path Expansion / Logit Attribution
concepts.summary: The technique of tracing a single linear path from an internal direction all the way to the logits, taken from the transformer circuits framework.
concepts.explanation: The [[logit-weight]] is computed following the path expansion approach of the Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits, also called logit attribution. The idea is to expand the network's computation into a sum of paths and read off the one path running from the [[feature-direction]], through the MLP output weights and unembedding, to the logits — ignoring the rest. This gives a first-order account of the feature's effect that the paper then checks against actual ablation. The paper notes related work in attribution patching.

citedFrom.refText: Elhage, Nelson et al. (2021). A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits. Transformer Circuits Thread
citedFrom.whyNeeded: Path expansion and the linearized layer norm treatment are defined there; this paper applies the recipe without deriving it, and the validity of the logit weight numbers depends on it.

concepts.name: Unembedding matrix
concepts.summary: The final linear map from the residual stream to one logit per vocabulary token.
concepts.explanation: The matrix $W_{unembed}$ turns the final residual stream vector into a logit for every token in the vocabulary. It is the last factor in the paper's [[logit-weight]] product, which is what lets a [[feature-direction]] be pushed all the way to the output.

concepts.name: Weight Interference
concepts.summary: The paper's hypothesis that the large central mode of near-zero logit weights is unwanted noise forced by superposition, not deliberate behavior.
concepts.explanation: When the paper plots a feature's logit weights, a few tokens stand out and the rest form a near-isotropic spread around zero. It reads that spread as the residue of superposition — the price of packing features into non-orthogonal directions. Two consequences follow. First, the existence of interference weights is itself counted as evidence for superposition. Second, the model may simply not care about these effects, since the tokens involved were already implausible for other reasons — suppressed by the [[direct-path]], the attention layer, or other MLP features. That is why [[logit-weight]] correlations between models can be low even when the features are doing the same job.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: When logit weights disagree but features match
concepts.summary: The extreme case: two features with activation correlation 0.98 and a negative logit weight correlation that are nonetheless doing the same job.
concepts.explanation: A/1/3949 and B/1/3321 both fire on 'pone' — and occasionally 'pgen' and 'pcbi' — as abbreviations for PLoS journal names in citations like @pone.0082392, and both predict the '.' that follows. Zooming in on the [[logit-weight]] scatterplot shows only the '.' token has high weight in both models; everything else sits in the interference portion of the distribution. The paper's reading is that the model may simply not care what a feature does to tokens that were already implausible, having been suppressed by the [[direct-path]], the attention layer, or other MLP features. It notes in passing that the feature firing on 0.02% of tokens implies at least 1 in 10,000 Pile tokens is a PLoS abbreviation — a fact about the dataset surfaced by a feature.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Explanation-Based Loss Measurement
concepts.summary: A proposed better measure — replacing activations with those predicted from natural-language explanations — that the paper judges computationally impractical for now.
concepts.explanation: Rather than replacing MLP activations with the autoencoder's reconstruction, one could replace them with activations simulated from the features' written explanations, which would test the interpretations rather than just the reconstruction. The paper notes others in the community have been considering this. Its objection is cost: naively, simulating a layer with 100k features means sampling the explaining model once per feature per token, which it estimates at roughly \$12,500–\$25,000 for a single 4,096-token context at then-current prices, over many contexts. It suggests approximations may exist, and separately raises the possibility of formalizing feature importance as an independent loss contribution per feature.

sections.title: How much of the model does our interpretation explain?

concepts.name: Why 79% Should Be Read Cautiously
concepts.summary: The paper's own reasons for distrusting its headline number: fraction-of-loss may be the wrong framing, and the features are not fully monosemantic.
concepts.explanation: The biggest issue the paper names is that framing the question in terms of fraction of loss may be misleading, because of the long tail: as the fraction explained rises, more and more features are needed to explain the residual, so a high percentage may correspond to a small fraction of the features. It also notes it does not believe its features are completely monosemantic — some polysemanticity may be hiding in low activations — nor that all of them are cleanly interpretable. Against this it sets the case studies, where ablating a feature decreases probabilities in the appropriate way and artificially activating it produces the corresponding behavior. The paper calls measuring how much a feature-based interpretation explains a model an important open question needing work on both defining metrics and computing them.

sections.title: How much of the model does our interpretation explain?

concepts.name: Why the Percentage Is an Overestimate
concepts.summary: The paper says the ablated-MLP baseline may be an especially bad one, so the fraction explained is likely inflated.
concepts.explanation: A transformer with its MLP removed is a badly damaged model, so the denominator in the normalization may be much larger than the amount of interesting work the MLP does. The paper flags the percentage as an overestimate for this reason, and reports ad hoc experiments — data not shown — in which similarly high percentages were reached simply by training a transformer from scratch with a small MLP. This is the paper hedging its own headline number rather than defending it.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

concepts.name: Zero-Ablation Baseline
concepts.summary: The loss increase from substitution is divided by the loss increase from removing the MLP layer entirely, giving a percentage of the MLP's contribution explained.
concepts.explanation: To express reconstruction quality as a fraction, the paper needs a scale for how much the MLP is worth at all. Zero-ablating the MLP — removing its contribution entirely — gives that scale. The autoencoder's extra loss is then measured against it, so "79% recovered" means the reconstruction gets back 79% of the gap between no MLP and the real MLP. The number depends entirely on this choice of baseline.

sections.title: How much of the model does our interpretation explain?
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

concepts.name: Activation Interval
concepts.summary: One of eleven evenly spaced bands between zero and a feature's maximum activation, used to sample examples uniformly across the whole activation spectrum rather than just the top.
concepts.explanation: The paper divides each feature's activation spectrum into eleven bands evenly spaced from zero activation to the maximum activation, and samples uniformly from them. This is the unit of analysis for both the manual scoring and the [[automated-interpretability]] work, and the appendix describes a thirteen-interval version used for prompt construction. The purpose is to defeat a specific failure mode: many polysemantic neurons look monosemantic if you only inspect their [[top-dataset-examples]] and are revealed as polysemantic lower down the spectrum. Sampling by interval forces the whole spectrum into view and makes it possible to ask how interpretability changes with activation strength.

concepts.name: Blinded Annotation
concepts.summary: The annotator scored features and neurons without knowing which kind of unit was being shown.
concepts.explanation: Because the comparison being made is between features and neurons, and the annotator is one of the paper's own authors, the scoring was done blind to unit type. This controls for the obvious risk that an author who wants features to win would score them more generously. It does not control for the sample being small, or for the annotator and the paper sharing a prior notion of what an interpretable unit looks like.

concepts.name: Feature Interpretability Rubric
concepts.summary: The 0–14 scoring scheme combining confidence in an interpretation, consistency of activations, consistency of logit weights, effect-size separation, and specificity.
concepts.explanation: The annotator first forms an interpretation from the positive logits and the activations across all intervals, then scores: confidence in the interpretation (0–3), consistency of the high-activation tokens with it (0–5), consistency of the positive logit effects with it (0–3), whether inconsistent logit effects were at least separated in effect size from consistent ones (0 or 1), and how specific the interpretation is (0–3). The total is the sum. The maximum is 14 rather than 15, because a perfect score on the logit consistency item makes the effect-size-separation item inapplicable. The paper says, very subjectively, that features scoring above 8 were quite interpretable. Note that the rubric includes logit interpretability, which is why the [[randomized-transformer]] scores badly here even where automated activation scoring flatters it.

concepts.name: From Cherry-Picked Features To Global Claims
concepts.summary: The turn in section 4 from four hand-chosen features to the population of all features, and the questions the paper says it cannot yet answer.
concepts.explanation: Section 4's stated aim is to ask how interpretable the rest of the features are, given that section 3 dealt only in cherry-picked cases. Its answer is that both humans and language models find features significantly more interpretable than neurons, and quite interpretable in absolute terms. The paper also names questions it cannot answer to its satisfaction: whether [[dictionary-learning]] is discovering all the features needed to understand the MLP layer, and how much of the layer's mechanics have been made interpretable — offering only preliminary speculation. All of this is computed after excluding A/1's 168 dead and 292 ultralow density features from the 4,096.

sections.title: How Interpretable is the Typical Feature?

concepts.name: Caveats on the Interpretability Evaluations
concepts.summary: Two acknowledged weaknesses in the manual and automated experiments: most activations fall in the less-interpretable low intervals, and features were sampled without regard to importance.
concepts.explanation: The paper lists both and then argues neither changes the conclusion, based on its own inspection of many features rather than on a further experiment. It also points readers at the interactive visualization for A/1 and the corresponding neurons, suggesting they sort by 'random' for an unbiased sample and run their own version of the experiment, or sort by importance metrics such as max activation and max density to test the second caveat themselves.

concepts.name: The Maximal-Example Weakness
concepts.summary: The evaluation flaw the paper is correcting for: judging a unit only by its top-activating examples makes polysemantic units look monosemantic.
concepts.explanation: The paper names this as a weakness it perceives in its own prior work, citing the SoLU paper, where evaluation focused predominantly on maximal dataset examples with less attention to the rest of the activation spectrum. Many polysemantic neurons look clean at the top and only reveal their mixture lower down. Sampling by [[activation-interval]] is the direct fix. The same concern shapes the automated setup, where the paper deliberately departs from Bills et al.'s scoring mixture.

citedFrom.refText: Elhage, Nelson et al. (2022). Softmax Linear Units. Transformer Circuits Thread
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The evaluation methodology being criticized is that paper's own; understanding what was done differently requires it.

concepts.name: Top activating dataset examples
concepts.summary: The standard inspection method: collect the datapoints on which a unit fires most strongly and read off what they have in common.
concepts.explanation: Used throughout, and published for all features of 90 learned dictionaries in the accompanying visualizations. The method carries a known weakness the paper works around: an interpretation fitted to the strongest examples may not describe the feature's typical or weak behavior, which is why the paper also uses interval sampling, causal tests, and off-distribution probes elsewhere. It is also how the paper establishes that some features are invisible in the neuron basis — the [[hebrew-feature]] has no counterpart in any neuron's top examples. In Section 5.2.2 it is the tool that reveals A/1/1544 fires on base64 that decodes to ASCII.

concepts.name: Circuit
concepts.summary: A subgraph of a network's computation — a set of components connected by weights — that implements some identifiable behavior.
concepts.explanation: In this line of work a circuit is a group of features or neurons wired together through the model's weights so that one component's output feeds another's input, jointly implementing a behavior. The paper's stated goal for feature decomposition is to enable 'basic circuit analysis'. It matters later that the '[[finite-state-automata-features|finite state automata]]' assemblies it finds are explicitly *not* circuits in this sense: those features connect through the sampled token stream rather than through weights within a forward pass.

concepts.name: Curse of dimensionality in interpretability
concepts.summary: As models grow, the volume of internal-state space that has to be interpreted grows exponentially, so the space cannot be searched or enumerated unless it decomposes into independent pieces.
concepts.explanation: The paper gives this as the key obstacle to reverse-engineering larger models. Its point is not that there are more numbers to look at but that the latent space's volume grows exponentially in its dimension, so no exhaustive inspection is possible. The only route the authors see is decomposition into independent components each of which can be understood on its own — which is what motivates looking for features.

concepts.name: Scalability of analysis
concepts.summary: The barrier that would remain even if sparse autoencoders fully solved superposition: turning microscopic feature-level insight into a macroscopic understanding of a model.
concepts.explanation: The authors ask directly whether solving superposition would be a home run and answer no — at least one other fundamental barrier remains. [[automated-interpretability]] is one candidate route, though they say delegating the understanding of AI to AI may not be fully satisfying for various reasons. The alternative they gesture at is discovering larger-scale structure among features, so that analysis can operate on groups rather than individual features.

concepts.name: Randomized Transformer Baseline
concepts.summary: Dictionary learning run on a one-layer model whose weights have been randomly shuffled, used to ask how much of the features' structure comes from the data rather than the model.
concepts.explanation: The paper runs its whole pipeline on a version of the run A transformer with randomized weights, so that any structure in the resulting features must come from the dataset rather than from learned computation. The resulting features contain many single-token features — "span", "file", ".", "nature" — and some features firing on seemingly arbitrary subsets of broadly recognizable contexts such as LaTeX or code. The paper reports it was unable to construct sensible interpretations for the non-single-token features and invites readers to check for themselves, concluding that the model's learning process creates richer structure in its activations than the token distribution alone. Used as an ablation for the interpretability scores, it produces one uncomfortable result: on automated activation scoring the randomized features have a higher median score than the real ones.

sections.title: Do features tell us about the model or the data?

concepts.name: The three base64 features
concepts.summary: A/1/2357 fires preferentially on letters in base64, A/1/2364 on digits, and A/1/1544 on base64 that decodes to ASCII text — jointly covering the single base64 feature of A/0.
concepts.explanation: The first two predict largely the same tokens with one difference: the digit feature has much lower logit weights for predicting digits. The third was harder to pin down; the clue was that it responds strongly to the token 'ICAgICAg', which decodes to six spaces. Checking [[top-dataset-examples]] confirmed that A/1/1544's examples contain substrings decoding to ASCII while the other two features' examples do not. Deciding whether a span decodes to ASCII is itself subtle, since base64 decodes in groups of four characters to triples of ASCII, so the authors select substrings that yield the maximal number of printable ASCII characters under a standard decoder.

concepts.name: Resetting Optimizer State on Resampling
concepts.summary: Adam's moment estimates are reset for every weight and bias changed by resampling.
concepts.explanation: Adam carries running estimates of gradient mean and variance per parameter, accumulated over the whole run. A resampled neuron's parameters have just been replaced with something unrelated, so the inherited moment estimates describe a parameter that no longer exists and would distort the first updates after the swap. The paper resets them for every modified weight and bias term.

concepts.name: Dead Neurons
concepts.summary: Autoencoder hidden units with zero activation across a large number of datapoints. They waste dictionary capacity, so the paper resamples them.
concepts.explanation: A hidden unit whose pre-ReLU input is negative on essentially every datapoint contributes nothing to reconstruction and receives no gradient, so it stays dead. Every dead neuron is a dictionary slot not representing a feature, which is why the paper says resampling lets the model represent more features for a given hidden layer dimension. The paper reports that the number of dead neurons depends on learning rate (too high), batch size (too low), dataset redundancy such as too many tokens per context or repeated epochs, the number of training steps (too many), and the optimizer used, and says this agrees with prior work on the emergence of sparse representations.

citedFrom.refText: Bricken, Trenton and Schaeffer, Rylan and Olshausen, Bruno and Kreiman, Gabriel. Emergence of Sparse Representations from Noise.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The paper says its findings on what causes dead neurons agree with this work but does not reproduce the underlying analysis.

concepts.name: Sampling by Squared Loss
concepts.summary: Resampled neurons are seeded from inputs chosen with probability proportional to the square of the autoencoder's current loss on them.
concepts.explanation: The point of resampling is to spend the freed capacity where the autoencoder is currently failing, so the seed input is drawn from a distribution weighted toward badly reconstructed datapoints. Squaring the loss sharpens that preference. The paper describes the design intent as seeding new features to fit the inputs where the current autoencoder performs worst.

concepts.name: Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
concepts.summary: The idea that a trained network's performance comes from a subnetwork whose initialization happened to be favorable. The paper offers it as a possible reason resampling helps.
concepts.explanation: The paper suggests resampling 'may be compatible with' the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis, on the reading that each resampled neuron is an extra draw at a favorable initialization, increasing the number of chances the network has to find promising feature directions. This is offered as a speculation about mechanism, not a tested claim — the paper provides no experiment separating this account from any other. The hypothesis itself comes from the cited work on finding sparse trainable subnetworks.

citedFrom.refText: Frankle, Jonathan and Carbin, Michael. The lottery ticket hypothesis: Finding sparse, trainable neural networks. arXiv:1803.03635
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The hypothesis is invoked by name as a possible explanation for why resampling works; its content is entirely in the cited paper.

concepts.name: Weak Initialization of the Resampled Encoder
concepts.summary: A revived neuron's encoder vector is scaled to 0.2 times the average live-neuron encoder norm and its bias set to zero, so it fires only weakly at first.
concepts.explanation: If a resampled neuron came back at full strength it would immediately start firing across many inputs and disturb features the autoencoder had already learned. Scaling its encoder down and zeroing its bias means it fires weakly and only for inputs similar to the one it was seeded from. The paper calls resetting the encoder norm and bias crucial, specifically to minimize interference with the rest of the network.

concepts.name: Byte-pair encoding
concepts.summary: The tokenizer scheme that merges frequent byte sequences into single tokens, so a token need not line up with a character.
concepts.explanation: Tokens are built by repeatedly merging the most frequent adjacent pairs in the training corpus. Two consequences matter here: a non-Latin Unicode character can be split across several byte tokens, and a common multi-character string can be a single token, which is why several of the paper's features are shaped by tokenization rather than by content.

concepts.name: Approximately Linear Logit Effects
concepts.summary: In a one-layer model, the effect of a feature on the output logits is close to linear in its activation, which makes downstream analysis tractable.
concepts.explanation: With a single layer, an MLP activation feeds the logits through what is nearly a linear path, so a feature's contribution to the output can be read approximately as its activation times a fixed vector of logit effects. The paper uses this to check that features reflect the model's function and not just structure in the data. It also names the double edge in a footnote: this linear structure makes the [[linear-representation-hypothesis]] more likely to hold here, and correspondingly makes the results less likely to generalize to multilayer models. Its counterweight is that others have found interpretable linear features with sparse autoencoders on multilayer transformers.

citedFrom.refText: Cunningham, Hoagy (2023). AutoInterpretation Finds Sparse Coding Beats Alternatives; also Smith, Logan (2023), Found 600+ Monosemantic Features in a Small LM Using Sparse Autoencoders and Really Strong Features Found in Residual Stream.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: These are the multilayer sparse autoencoder results the paper leans on to argue its one-layer findings generalize; the evidence is entirely in them.

concepts.name: MLP Activations as the Decomposition Target
concepts.summary: A one-layer attention-only transformer can be analyzed by rewriting it without reference to hidden states; adding a ReLU MLP makes that impossible, so the MLP activations are the state you cannot avoid decomposing.
concepts.explanation: In A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits the authors analyzed a one-layer attention-only network by rewriting it in terms of weight products, sidestepping hidden activations entirely. That trick fails as soon as a ReLU MLP is present, because the nonlinearity cannot be folded away. The paper therefore calls a one-layer transformer with an MLP 'the simplest language model we profoundly don't understand' and takes its 512-dimensional MLP activations as the thing to decompose into features.

citedFrom.refText: Elhage, Nelson et al. (2021). A Mathematical Framework for Transformer Circuits. Transformer Circuits Thread
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The claim that an attention-only one-layer model can be understood without decomposing hidden states rests entirely on the rewriting done in that paper.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Dataset and Basic Training

concepts.name: Overtraining the Transformer
concepts.summary: Training the small model on far more tokens than compute-optimal, on the hypothesis that this yields cleaner representations in superposition.
concepts.explanation: The paper trains a one-layer model on 100 billion tokens, which it can afford precisely because the model is small. Its stated hypothesis is that a very high number of training tokens may allow the model to learn cleaner representations in superposition. This is offered as a reason for the design choice, not as something the paper tests — there is no comparison against a less-trained transformer.

concepts.name: The Pile
concepts.summary: The public 800GB text corpus the transformers are trained on, chosen over Anthropic's internal dataset for reproducibility.
concepts.explanation: The paper says it trained on the Pile specifically so that its experiments would be more reproducible by others. It also flags a consequence for interpreting the results: while it thinks many features are universal, others are very likely idiosyncratic to the dataset — so a feature found here is not automatically a feature of language models in general. The Pile is also the source of the 40 million contexts used to build the autoencoder's activation dataset.

citedFrom.refText: Leo Gao et al. (2020). The Pile: An 800GB Dataset of Diverse Text for Language Modeling.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: What is actually in the Pile determines which features exist at all — the paper's base64, DNA and Arabic script features depend on the corpus composition described in the cited work.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Dataset and Basic Training

concepts.name: Residual stream
concepts.summary: The running vector each block reads from and writes back into; here it is 128-dimensional.
concepts.explanation: The transformer's blocks add their outputs into a shared vector that runs from the embedding to the unembedding. In the model studied here it has 128 dimensions, while the MLP it feeds has 512 neurons, so the MLP layer is where the paper looks for features.

concepts.name: The A and B Transformers
concepts.summary: A second one-layer transformer with the same architecture, data and hyperparameters as the first, differing only in random seed, with its own dictionary learning run B/1.
concepts.explanation: B is a transformer trained on the same data as A but from a different random initialization, and B/1 is a [[dictionary-learning-run]] on it. Because the two models share the dataset but not the initialization, a feature appearing in both is evidence about how one-layer transformers represent this data, not about one accident of optimization. The paper is careful about how much this shows: same architecture and same dataset means it does not establish universality across architectures or data distributions. The base64 case reaches slightly further, since a base64 neuron had already been found in a differently trained SoLU model.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Undercomplete basis
concepts.summary: A feature set smaller than the dimension of the space being decomposed — what earlier dictionary learning work on transformers recovered.
concepts.explanation: Yun et al. applied [[dictionary-learning]] to the residual stream of a 12-layer transformer and found an undercomplete basis of features. The paper flags this as the contrast with its own approach: if superposition is real, the interesting features are precisely the ones an undercomplete dictionary cannot hold, so expanding past the layer width is the point.

citedFrom.refText: Yun, Zeyu and Chen, Yubei and Olshausen, Bruno A and LeCun, Yann. Transformer visualization via dictionary learning: contextualized embedding as a linear superposition of transformer factors. arXiv:2103.15949
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The prior state of the art for dictionary learning on transformer activations, and the setting this paper's expansion factors are defined against.

concepts.name: Classic Examples of Polysemanticity
concepts.summary: The concrete examples the paper offers of what polysemanticity looks like: a neuron mixing citations, dialogue, HTTP requests and Korean, and the vision neuron responding to cat faces and car fronts.
concepts.explanation: To fix what it means to rule out, the paper gives two examples. In its own one-layer transformer, one neuron responds to a mix of academic citations, English dialogue, HTTP requests and Korean text. In vision models there is the classic case of a neuron responding to both cat faces and the fronts of cars. Both share a signature: clearly unrelated concepts in one unit. This is why the paper treats specificity as the key test — a feature that fires only in one rare, specific context cannot be polysemantic in this way.

citedFrom.refText: Olah, Chris and Mordvintsev, Alexander and Schubert, Ludwig (2017). Feature Visualization. Distill
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The cat-face/car-front neuron and the feature visualization methods that revealed it come from there.

concepts.name: Mechanistic interpretability
concepts.summary: The program of understanding a neural network by breaking it into components that are easier to understand than the whole, then reasoning about how those components interact.
concepts.explanation: The paper opens by stating this agenda: identify the right components, understand what each does, understand how they combine, and from that reason about the network's behavior. The first step is picking the components, and the paper's argument is that the obvious choice — the neuron — is the wrong one. Decomposition is treated as a means, not the end: once you have components you still have to trace circuits and build a larger-scale picture. The paper is explicit that decomposing a model is 'just the beginning of the work'.

concepts.name: Monosemanticity
concepts.summary: The property of a unit responding to one coherent thing, so that a single interpretation covers when it fires and what it does.
concepts.explanation: The paper's title names this as a direction rather than an achieved state — 'towards' monosemanticity. A monosemantic unit has an activation condition you can state and a downstream effect consistent with that condition. The claim made is comparative and hedged: the learned features are 'relatively monosemantic' and offer 'a more monosemantic unit of analysis than the model's neurons themselves'. The authors do not claim their interpretations capture every aspect of a feature's behavior.

concepts.name: Polysemanticity and capacity
concepts.summary: A mathematical framework, from prior work, for when a network prefers monosemantic versus polysemantic representations.
concepts.explanation: Cited in Related Work as one of the developments since Toy Models. Its relevance here is the result the paper borrows in Section 2.3: under mean squared error loss and certain feature importance curves, models may actively prefer the monosemantic solution. That is the contrast case against which the paper argues that cross-entropy-trained language models will not.

citedFrom.refText: Scherlis, Adam and Sachan, Kshitij and Jermyn, Adam S and Benton, Joe and Shlegeris, Buck. Polysemanticity and capacity in neural networks. arXiv:2210.01892
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The claim that some loss functions prefer monosemantic solutions is imported wholesale; the conditions under which it holds live in that paper.

concepts.name: The four-feature loss calculation
concepts.summary: A toy calculation showing a single binary neuron gets lower cross-entropy loss by firing on two features ambiguously than on one feature cleanly.
concepts.explanation: Setup: one neuron, four mutually exclusive features A/B/C/D, each predicting its own next token, and the neuron either fires or does not. If it fires only on A and predicts A correctly, it must predict uniformly over B/C/D the rest of the time, giving loss $\frac{3}{4}\ln 3 \approx 0.8$. If instead it fires on both A and B and predicts uniformly over A and B, while predicting uniformly over C and D when silent, the loss is $\ln 2 \approx 0.7$. The polysemantic option wins. The authors note this looks like a story about one neuron but argue it is the general situation at the sparsity limit.

concepts.name: Bounce Plots
concepts.summary: A toy-model diagnostic the paper uses to check whether the autoencoder is behaving correctly. Failure to produce them is what motivated adding biases.
concepts.explanation: The paper refers back to plots it calls 'bounce plots' from its toy-model investigations, and reports that on toy problems with a bias the autoencoder would not produce them unless a learned bias was added at both the decoder output and the encoder input. The reproduced text does not restate what the plots show, so the term is used here only as the symptom that the modification fixed. It is worth reading as evidence of the kind the paper offers throughout this appendix — anecdotal and toy-model-based rather than a controlled ablation on the real autoencoder.

concepts.name: Geometric Median Initialization
concepts.summary: The tied bias is initialized to the geometric median of the activation dataset — the point minimizing summed Euclidean distance to all datapoints.
concepts.explanation: Rather than starting the bias at zero, the paper starts it at the geometric median of the activations, so the autoencoder begins already centered on the bulk of the data. The geometric median is the point minimizing the sum of L2 distances to the dataset, which makes it less sensitive to outlying activations than the mean would be. The paper states the choice without ablating it separately.

concepts.name: Kurtosis as a privileged-basis test
concepts.summary: Using the heavy-tailedness of weights in the neuron basis as evidence that the basis is singled out, even when individual features spread across many neurons.
concepts.explanation: Reported in the [[external-replication]]. If feature directions were oriented at random, their coordinates in the neuron basis would look Gaussian; excess kurtosis indicates the coordinates concentrate more than chance on particular neurons. The replicator found decoder weights highly distributed — most features not explained by any small set of neurons — and still found kurtosis indicating a [[privileged-basis]], which he describes as surprising.

concepts.name: Bimodality of Randomized Features
concepts.summary: The randomized model's features split into a single-token cluster and a polysemantic cluster; once separated, the real features win on the second.
concepts.explanation: The [[randomized-transformer]]'s automated scores are distinctly bimodal. Splitting them out, the single-token cluster scores very highly and drives the misleading median, while the non-single-token cluster has a distribution similar to that of the polysemantic neurons — and there the A/1 features score higher. The same split appears in the manual human scores, with a cluster at 0 matching the polysemantic neurons and a non-zero cluster. In the manual case that non-zero cluster still scores worse than A/1 features, because the rubric includes logit interpretability, which is zero for a shuffled model. This is the paper's explanation for the one metric on which its features lose.

concepts.name: Single Token Features
concepts.summary: Features where the same token carries the largest activation in all twenty top-interval examples; abundant in the randomized model and trivially easy to explain and score.
concepts.explanation: The paper's example is a high-magnitude feature firing on the token ' P' wherever it starts a word. These are puzzling because the model could get the same effect from different bigram statistics and so has no reason to spend MLP capacity on them; similar features were also reported in prior work on the residual stream. [[feature-splitting]] is offered as the explanation: the model has not learned one 'P' feature but many features firing on P in different contexts, with different effects on neurons and logits, and a coarse dictionary cannot tell them apart. Allowing more features resolves them into what the paper calls a zoo of different P features. In this case the refined features were found by [[manual-inspection]] rather than by cosine similarity.

concepts.name: Weight Shuffling
concepts.summary: The randomization method: shuffle the entries within each weight matrix of the trained model rather than resampling them.
concepts.explanation: The random model is generated by randomly shuffling the entries of each weight matrix of the trained transformer used in run A. Shuffling rather than resampling guarantees that the distribution of individual weights matches the trained model exactly, so any difference between the two must be due to structure — which entries sit where — rather than to scale or distributional differences. This makes it a tighter control than a freshly initialized network.

sections.title: Do features tell us about the model or the data?

concepts.name: Activation-mass (expected value) plot
concepts.summary: A feature's activation histogram with each bin weighted by activation magnitude instead of counted once per token, so a bar's height is total activation contributed rather than number of firings. It answers where a feature's influence on the model comes from, not how often it fires.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The claim on the table is [[activation-specificity]] for the [[arabic-script-feature]]: when this feature fires, the text is Arabic script. The paper has a number for it — 81% of the tokens the feature is active on score as Arabic under an independent [[computational-proxy]], against a 0.13% base rate — and the [[feature-activation-distribution-plot]] behind it. Both count every firing once, the wrong weighting for the claim. A [[feature]] fires at 0.2 on some tokens and at 7 on others, and in this one-layer model a feature's contribution to the logits is approximately linear in its activation ([[linear-logit-effects]]), so those firings do not matter equally to the model's behaviour. The paper states this as [[large-activations-dominate]].

That matters because the impure region is also the crowded one: about 25% Arabic where the feature is barely on, about 98% above activation 5. A count histogram is tallest exactly where the interpretation is weakest, and a single average inherits that bias without showing it. A table of purity per band would give percentages but not say how much of the feature's output each band supplies. Multiplying each bin's count by its activation level is the smallest change that puts frequency and consequence in one picture. The paper calls the result an [[expected-value-plot]], taking the device from Cammarata et al.'s curve detector work. What it assumes rather than shows is that magnitude is the right currency: firm for one layer, the paper says, and conjectural for deeper models.

### How to read it, step by step

Two of the three encodings are copied from the companion histogram, which is the trap. The horizontal axis is the same [[feature-activation]] level — the post-ReLU scalar the [[sparse-autoencoder]] assigns to this feature's direction on a token — from just above zero to 9, with exact zeros left out because the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] makes them the overwhelming majority. The colour is the same stacked split by the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log(P(s\mid\text{Arabic Script})/P(s))$: deep blue at $-5$, white at $0$, deep red at $+5$, the legend printed on the companion.

Only the vertical axis changed, and it is no longer a token count. A bin's height is how many tokens landed in it times how hard the feature fired on them: total activation contributed, in units (0K to 35K) set by the sample size. Read the shape and the colour split, not the number.

Check the difference by hand, with both charts open. At the far left the companion peaks above 5K tokens and is visibly blue; here the curve is on the floor, because a large count times an activation near zero is almost nothing. Near 6.9 the companion has a lower hump of roughly 4.7K, and $4.7\text{K} \times 6.9 \approx 32\text{K}$ — this chart's peak. Then read the blue as a fraction of column height, not as a width.

### What a bad result would look like

Mass piled on the left and decaying rightward: the feature's influence coming from its weak, impure firings, with the 98%-pure region a sliver doing almost none of the work. Or blue keeping a broad share of the area after weighting, meaning non-Arabic strings drive the feature hard — [[polysemanticity]] surviving the test rather than being excluded by it. Or red filling every activation level, which would say the proxy calls most text Arabic and proves nothing. The figure shows mass concentrated between 5 and 8, blue reduced to a hairline.

It does not adjudicate the [[weak-activation-hypotheses]]; it argues only that whichever is right, that tail carries little weight. It cannot separate [[proxy-false-negatives]] at high activation from real non-Arabic firing. And the weighting is a choice, not a neutral view.

### Where it comes back

As a drawn figure, once: fig-9, always read against its companion. The DNA, base64 and Hebrew case studies get the unweighted spectrum only, the argument carried over rather than redrawn, so this evidence exists for one feature. The move returns twice more. [[activation-interval-analysis]] scores each band of the spectrum separately, then uses the same large-activations argument to discount the low bands. [[importance-scoring]] re-weights the other way, toward what random text would give, and there the correction makes features look worse, not better.

concepts.name: Activation spectrum coloured by a proxy
concepts.summary: A histogram of one unit's activation values across sampled tokens, with each column split by an independently computed score for whether that text matches the hypothesis about the unit. It is the paper's standard test of whether a unit fires only in the context claimed for it, and it reads by proportion within a column, not by bar height.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The question behind every one of these figures is whether a unit fires *only* in the context someone has hypothesised for it — what the paper calls [[activation-specificity]], and the main thing that would rule out [[polysemanticity]]. A single percentage could answer that, and the paper does quote one: Arabic script is 0.13% of training tokens but 81% of the tokens where the Arabic feature is on. That number hides the thing the paper actually wants to say. Specificity is not constant along the firing range; it climbs from about 25% at the bottom to about 98% above activation 5. An average over all firings is dominated by the many weak ones, which are the least pure and — because a [[feature]] acts linearly on the logits — the least consequential ([[large-activations-dominate]]). A bar chart or a table of category counts would collapse the activation axis and lose exactly that gradient.

The second reason is independence. The colour is not something the model reports. It is a [[computational-proxy]] computed from the token string alone. Laying the two side by side turns the picture into a joint distribution of two quantities produced by separate machinery, which is the form an argument about a unit's meaning has to take. It also lets the paper show its own bad cases rather than reporting one flattering number.

### How to read it, step by step

The horizontal axis is the [[feature-activation]]: the ReLU output of one hidden unit of the [[sparse-autoencoder]] on one token, running from just above zero out to roughly 7–12 depending on the feature. Exact zeros are not plotted. They sit in the small `0` / `>0` control at the far left, because the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] makes hard zeros the overwhelming majority and would put a spike at the origin. Everything you see is therefore already conditioned on the unit firing at all.

The vertical axis is density: how many sampled tokens land in each bin. Note its magnitude — features peak around 5K–40K, the neuron plots around 1.4M. That gap is itself evidence about how often each unit fires.

Colour is the proxy score, a [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log(P(s\mid H)/P(s))$ maximised over prefixes ending at the token ([[prefix-maximization]]), clipped to $\pm 5$: deep blue at $-5$, white at $0$, deep red at $+5$. Within each vertical slice the tokens are stacked by that score, reddest at the bottom, so one column is a small stacked bar, and the claim lives in the red *fraction* band by band.

Look first at the thin strip beneath the main panel, which renormalises every column to full height. Read it left to right: does red take over as activation rises? Then check the main panel's height where it does, so you know the red end is not three tokens. Then the four boxes on top, five random dataset examples each ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]), where orange shading means activation, not proxy score.

The habitual misreading is the tall spike just above zero. It is a count of weak firings, not a statement that the unit is mostly about non-Arabic.

### What a bad result would look like

A polysemantic unit gives a conditional strip that is flat: the same red-blue sandwich at 0.5 as at 8. The paper draws that version itself, in the neuron figures — [[most-correlated-neuron]] plots that stay blue across the whole range with a red sliver that never grows ([[feature-neuron-nonalignment]]). A second failure is red arriving only in a tail with no mass under it. A third is red everywhere including at zero, which would mean the proxy fires on most text and proves nothing.

The honest caveat runs the other way too. Blue surviving at high activation is read by the paper as the proxy's fault — punctuation inside Hebrew scores as non-Hebrew because it is outside the Unicode block ([[proxy-limitations]]) — and at low activation it offers three [[weak-activation-hypotheses]]. Those are judgements, not measurements. The proxy is a cheap yardstick, not ground truth about meaning.

### Where it comes back

Three jobs. As a feature's own specificity exhibit: fig-8 (Arabic), fig-20 (DNA, where the bimodal score is reduced to a yes/no by [[proxy-binarization]] and reported as a 0.8 correlation), fig-25 (base64), fig-33 (Hebrew). As a negative control on the nearest neuron: fig-14, fig-23, fig-30. And as the [[universality]] check, the same plot for the matched feature in the second transformer ([[transformer-a-and-b]]) found by [[activation-similarity]]: fig-17 (corr 0.91), fig-27 (0.85), fig-36 (0.92), where the picture, not a number, is the argument. What changes between them is the hypothesis and its proxy, the activation range, whether the proxy is graded or binarised, and the density scale. Figure 9 reuses the same axis with the histogram weighted by activation magnitude ([[expected-value-plot]]).
