concepts.name: Annotated dataset-example panel
concepts.summary: Dataset snippets laid out in cells by activation level, with two separate quantities drawn onto each token: orange shading for how hard the feature fires, and a coloured underline for how much that token's predicted log-likelihood moved when the feature was ablated. It is how the paper shows a feature's causal effect and audits feature-proxy disagreements case by case, by inspection and count rather than by measurement.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Two questions force this shape. Does a [[feature]] actually change what the model predicts, and on which tokens? And when a feature and an independent [[computational-proxy]] disagree, which is wrong? Neither is answerable by a number, because both are claims about *alignment*: that a measured quantity lands on exactly the tokens a reader would point to. No axis can encode "this token is Arabic script" — only the text does, so the text becomes the substrate and the measurements are drawn onto it.

A bar chart of mean logit change would say the [[arabic-script-feature]] helps Arabic predictions on average, and hide that the only tokens it *hurts* are punctuation shared with other scripts — the detail that makes the interpretation specific. An average flattens the second question too. The paper reports a Pearson correlation of $0.8$ between the binarized [[dna-proxy]] and the [[dna-feature]]'s activations; that says disagreement exists without saying whose fault it is. The grid exists so the authors can open each disagreement and assign blame.

### How to read it, step by step

There is no y-axis. The layout encodes conditions. Columns are bands of the feature's firing range: in fig-11 two [[activation-interval]]s, the top band and a middle one at about half that activation; in fig-21 four sampled levels, each tied by a dotted line to the activation histogram underneath. Rows, where there are two, carry a second variable — the proxy's yes/no verdict after [[proxy-binarization]].

Each cell holds five or six snippets. One snippet is a nine-token window — a bold selected token whose activation put the example in that cell, four tokens of context either side — drawn from a 100-million-token subset ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]).

Two independent encodings sit on the same token. Orange background is [[feature-activation]], the ReLU output of one [[sparse-autoencoder]] hidden unit, darker for stronger. The underline comes from a second forward pass in which the feature's activation times its [[feature-direction]] is subtracted from the MLP activations across the whole context ([[feature-ablation]]). It shows how far that token's predicted log-likelihood moved: purple or blue for a drop, meaning the feature had been helping; orange-red for a rise, meaning it had been hurting; flat grey for no change; thickness and saturation for size ([[ablation-effect-visualization]]). The scale is unlabelled, so compare underlines within a figure, not across.

Read the legend inset first, then the cells where feature and proxy agree, then the off-diagonal cells. In fig-11, Arabic glyphs render on a lower line while byte tokens that are only half a character appear above as escape codes, each with its own background and underline ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]).

### What a bad result would look like

For an ablation panel: underlines indifferent to the script, heavy purple under Latin tokens as often as Arabic ones; or every underline flat grey, meaning the direction is a fact about the data, not something the MLP uses; or the half-activation column carrying underlines as heavy as the full-activation column, which would break the roughly linear story the [[logit-weight]] picture assumes ([[large-activations-dominate]]).

For a disagreement grid: the cell where the proxy fires and the feature is off filled with plain nucleotide strings the feature simply missed ([[activation-sensitivity]]), and the feature-on, proxy-off row filled with ordinary English ([[activation-specificity]]). Then the blame would fall on the feature, and the correlation would be flattering it.

Judge the counting honestly: ten and forty-eight hand-read examples, adjudicated by the authors, on features the paper says were chosen for being easy to analyze ([[cherry-picked-case-studies]]). "One genuine error out of six" is a tally of a display, not an error rate on a population, and the attribution of the other twenty-two disagreements to [[proxy-limitations]] is a judgement.

### Where it comes back

fig-11 (3.1.3) is the ablation form: one feature, no proxy, columns as activation bands. fig-21 (3.2.1) is the audit form: random rather than top examples ([[top-dataset-examples]]), a proxy verdict on the rows, no underlines, and a histogram welded to the bottom. What changes is what the columns condition on and whether the underline encoding is present at all. The same annotated snippet is the atom of the [[feature-exploration-interface]]; fig-12 answers the causal question by generation instead ([[pinned-feature-sampling]]).

concepts.name: Conceptual schematic
concepts.summary: A cartoon of activation space or of an argument, drawn where the paper has a claim but no measurement for it yet. Its job is to fix what a hypothesis means, or what would count as evidence for one, so the reader can hold the picture against the measured figures that follow.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Four times the paper stops plotting and draws instead, each time for a claim with no measured quantity attached to it yet. Figure 3 says what the observed network is supposed to *be* — a squeezed-down projection of a larger, sparser one — which is [[superposition]], the hypothesis that a network represents more [[feature|features]] (interpretable directions in activation space) than it has neurons. Figure 7 says, before any evidence appears, what would count as ruling out [[polysemanticity]] — a single unit firing on clearly unrelated things. Figure 45 says what the geometry of [[feature-splitting]] should look like. Figure 62 asks whether a feature is a single direction at all.

A bar chart, an average or a table needs an axis with units and a population to average over. These four claims have a relation instead: inside or outside, more or fewer, the same territory or new territory, one description or two. Forcing a number onto them would hide that no number exists yet — figure 3 imports a hypothesis from earlier work, and figure 62 is conjecture the paper marks with "perhaps". A drawing wears that status on its face.

### How to read it, step by step

There are no axes, so start with the printed sentence beside or below the drawing: the words carry the claim, the picture illustrates it. Then find what changes between panels — that difference is the argument, the rest is scaffolding.

The vocabulary is small and reused. A dot is one unit — a neuron in figure 3, a token where a feature fires in figure 7, a [[feature-direction]] (the unit vector a feature writes along) in figures 45 and 62. An arrow is either a mapping — figure 3's orange dashed arrows run downward, meaning the larger network is expressed inside the smaller one — or a direction from the origin, as in figure 45, where all arrows share a tail because only their angles mean anything.

Colour does real work. Orange marks the operative element: the projection in figure 3, the boundary of the [[computational-proxy]] in figure 7, a score computed from the text alone, independent of the autoencoder. Grey means backdrop or conjectured; figure 45's faint arrows are the paper's imagined [[true-features]], held fixed across all three panels so you watch the bold learned ones multiply against them.

Then stop. Counting dots or reading positions as coordinates invents precision the drawing lacks. Figure 3's six-into-three squeeze stands for 4,096 features over 512 neurons; figure 62's four ring points are four because four spaces evenly.

### What a bad result would look like

Two of these draw the failure themselves. Figure 7's first panel *is* the bad case: dots scattered across the whole circle with no common region — the paper's example is a neuron responding to academic citations, English dialogue, HTTP requests and Korean text. That is a failure of [[activation-specificity]]. Figure 62's left panel deflates its own hypothesis: a manifold that is only the convex hull of features firing together is [[correlated-features]] renamed, not a rival account.

The other two you have to construct. Figure 3 fails if each neuron already is one clean feature — a [[privileged-basis]] — which would make [[dictionary-learning]] unnecessary. Figure 45 fails if widening the [[sparse-autoencoder]] sends the bold arrows out of the grey blob, or to wide angles from each other: new features rather than finer ones, and the [[feature-umap]] behind it would show no tight clusters.

None of this can be settled by looking; falsification lives in the measured figures each one points at.

### Where it comes back

What changes across the four is distance from evidence. Figure 3 opens the problem setup, borrowed. Figure 7 sets the standard the case studies are then held to, and its third panel is already a concession: features are often narrower than the proxy, so several share the region ([[multiple-features-for-one-context]]). Figure 45 arrives *after* the UMAP that measured it, summarising a result rather than announcing one. Figure 62 sits in the discussion with no experiment behind it, offered as one possible reason splitting never stopped, and why the [[correct-number-of-features]] may not be a well-posed question.

concepts.name: Cross-model agreement scatter with marginals
concepts.summary: A scatter in which every dot is a matched pair of features from two independently trained models — one axis the activation correlation used to choose the pair, the other a second, free measure of agreement — with a histogram of each axis along the edges. It is how the paper checks whether two different definitions of "the same feature" agree across a whole population rather than on chosen examples.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Section 5.3 asks whether the same [[feature|features]] form in two separately trained models — the paper's test of [[universality]]. It already has a headline number for that: the median [[activation-similarity|activation correlation]] between an A/1 feature and its closest partner in B/1 is $0.72$. These two figures ask a harder, second question, which no single number can answer: when you compare features by two different definitions of "the same feature", do the definitions agree on the same pairs?

That is a question about a joint distribution, so it needs a scatter. A bar chart or an average of each measure gives two levels and nothing about pairing — you could not tell whether the pairs that fire alike are the pairs that write alike, which is the whole point. A table of a few examples invites suspicion that they were chosen. The paper also needs both a population-wide pattern and one pair (A/1/3949 and B/1/3321) where the mechanism is visible; only a scatter shows both, with the outlier in view rather than averaged away.

### How to read it, step by step

One dot is **one matched pair of features**, not a token and not a vocabulary entry. This is the most common misreading: the per-feature comparison plots earlier in the paper look almost identical, and there each dot is a datapoint or a vocabulary token. Here, each [[sparse-autoencoder]] feature in run A/1 is paired with the run B/1 feature it correlates with most — B being a second one-layer transformer differing only in random seed ([[transformer-a-and-b]]), with its own dictionary. A/1 has 4,096 features, so the cloud holds a few thousand dots.

The horizontal axis is always activation correlation: the [[pearson-correlation]] between the two features' activation vectors over a fixed set of dataset tokens. That coordinate is also the criterion used to pick the partner, so every point is pushed as far right as that A/1 feature can get. The bottom marginal is therefore not "how similar are two features in general" but "how good was the best match available", and it should lean right.

The vertical axis is the only free measurement. In fig-53 it is [[logit-weight-similarity]], the correlation of the two features' [[logit-weight]] vectors over vocabulary. In fig-54 it is [[attribution-similarity]], the correlation of their [[attribution-vector|attribution vectors]].

Colour encodes nothing: both plots are monochrome, and density of overplotted grey is the only intensity channel. Colour appears only as annotation — the gold ring on the outlier, the red period label in fig-53's inset.

Look first at the diagonal $y = x$: both axes are correlations on the same $0$–$1$ scale, so it is meaningful. Then read the left marginal — where the free measure piles up, and whether it reaches $1.0$ at all.

### What a bad result would look like

For fig-54, whose claim is that attribution correlation tracks activation correlation, the failure case is a round blob with no tilt: pairs that fire together attributing no better than pairs that do not. A second failure is a band pinned near $1.0$ regardless of $x$, meaning attribution correlation is high for any pair and measures nothing. One caution the paper does not raise: the attribution vector has the activation as a factor, so the axes are not independent — some diagonal is built in.

Fig-53 inverts this: it is drawn to show a gap, so a tight diagonal would have meant no problem. What undercuts its reading is if the low points sat at low $x$ too — then they are bad matches rather than [[interference]] from [[superposition]] — or if the inset showed several large disagreeing tokens instead of one large agreeing one.

Neither plot can say whether $0.72$ is high; that needs the neuron baseline of $0.46$ from the companion histogram.

### Where it comes back

The shape appears twice in the same subsection, on the same population, with the same $x$. Only $y$ changes: logit weight correlation, then attribution correlation. Read them as a pair — the second is the repair of the first, and the change in cloud shape between them is the argument. The neighbouring [[feature-vs-neuron-universality|feature-versus-neuron histograms]] use the same matched pairs with the scatter dropped.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Per-feature dictionary diagnostic scatter
concepts.summary: A scatter in which every point is one learned feature, placed by numbers read off its own encoder and decoder vectors — how concentrated its direction is in the neuron basis, its bias, its decoder-encoder dot product, its density. It is for claims about a whole dictionary at once, made before anyone has interpreted a single feature.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Both figures make a claim about a whole dictionary at once, and both have to make it without knowing what any feature means. The only inputs are the autoencoder's own weights: per feature, one column of the [[dictionary-decoder]] and one row of the encoder. No tokens, no activations, no human reading. The numbers can be computed for every feature in a run, which is what the claims need: they are about the population, not about examples.

A summary number was available in each case and would have hidden the point. In the replication, the reported split — 4% of features dominated by a single neuron, 4% by their top ten, 92% neither — is the table version. The scatter shows those labels are threshold cuts through one continuous cloud, not three kinds of thing. In the density appendix an average is the wrong instrument: the claim is that features fall into two groups, and a mean sits between them. Two axes would not do either — the third diagnostic is added because no single one of the three pulls the groups apart alone.

### How to read it, step by step

One point is one feature, meaning one hidden unit of the [[sparse-autoencoder]], placed by numbers derived from its own weights.

In the decoder-sparsity version, square every entry of the feature's decoder column and divide by their total. The x-axis is the largest single share; the y-axis is shares two through ten added up. Both are fractions of the same total, so $x + y \le 1$, and no one of the next nine can beat the top one, so $y \le 9x$ — the straight diagonal edge cutting the upper left, above which nothing can sit. Colour is a label the author assigned by thresholding those shares (red 1-sparse, green 10-sparse, blue dense); the cutoffs are not printed, so colour is his reading drawn onto the plot rather than a separate measurement. Look at the marginal histograms first: the scatter overplots hardest where most features are.

In the three-diagnostic version, depth is [[feature-density]] on a $\log_{10}$ scale from $-10$ to $-3$, logarithmic because densities span that many orders of magnitude. Height is the feature's entry of the encoder bias $\mathbf{b}_e$ in $\mathbf{f} = \mathrm{ReLU}(W_e\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{b}_e)$ ([[autoencoder-encoder]]), always negative and readable as a firing threshold. The horizontal axis is the dot product of the feature's decoder column with its encoder row, which carries information only because the two are learned separately ([[untied-decoder-weights]]). Colour re-encodes depth. Look for the shape of the cloud, not for points: whether one compact blob stands clear of the large mass.

### What a bad result would look like

If learned features were mostly neurons wearing new names, the decoder-sparsity cloud would pile against the right edge, $x$ near 1 and $y$ near 0, with the top marginal spiking there. Instead the blue mass sits below $x = 0.2$ — the bulk form of what the case studies find one feature at a time ([[neuron-basis-coefficients]], [[features-invisible-in-the-neuron-basis]]), and what [[superposition]] predicts. The plot does not display the [[kurtosis-privileged-basis-test]] claim attached to it, that the [[privileged-basis]] survives anyway; that one comes from the text.

For the three-diagnostic version, failure is a gradient instead of an island — orange shading continuously into crimson with no gap, which is what density alone gives in large runs with a large [[l1-coefficient]] ([[feature-density-histogram]]). A single rendered angle can also fool you: a 3-D projection may open a gap that closes on rotation, and the reader gets one view. And separation, however clean, does not show the [[ultralow-density-cluster]] is a training artifact ([[density-cluster-separation]]); it supplies a boundary to draw, no more.

### Where it comes back

Twice, in different hands. Figure 63 sits in the [[external-replication]] section: two axes plus marginals, categorical colour, an outside researcher's dictionary, asking whether features are neurons. Figure 66 sits in the feature-density appendix: three axes, continuous colour, the authors' own run, asking whether the [[high-density-cluster]] can be fenced off — its darkest points, at the sparse extreme, being [[de-facto-dead-neurons]]. The reading habit holds across both: points are features, coordinates come from weights alone, and the evidence is where the cloud sits, never where a point sits.

concepts.name: Feature browser screenshot
concepts.summary: A screengrab of the paper's published feature browser with arrows and captions added: one page lays four separate kinds of evidence about a single learned feature side by side, and the search strip shows the queries the authors could put to a whole run. It is not one chart with one axis, and everything outside the grey panel is annotation the tool itself never prints.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The paper cannot argue its case one number at a time. Its per-feature argument is a fixed set of claims — the [[feature-evidence-template|five-claim template]] — and each claim comes in a different unit: a purity fraction, a next-token [[logit-weight]], a Pearson correlation against neurons, a firing rate. There is no shared axis, so there is no single plot. The browser lays the four kinds of evidence side by side on one screen and lets a reader see whether they agree about the same [[feature]]. A table of scores would have hidden the disagreements — a feature can look clean on its top examples and messy three bands down, and the layout keeps both in view.

The second reason is scale. Run A/1 has 4,096 features and the paper discusses four in depth. A bar chart of average interpretability would let the authors choose what to average and would inherit [[max-dataset-example-bias|the maximal-example problem]]: judge any unit by its strongest firings and it looks monosemantic. Publishing the browser hands the check to the reader, who can open a feature the paper never mentions. The search strip is the other half of that. It carries no results at all; what it establishes is the shape of query the authors could put to their own [[dictionary-learning-run|run]].

### How to read it, step by step

Everything outside the grey panel is annotation added for the paper. The [[feature-exploration-interface|interface]] prints none of it.

A feature page reads in four columns. First, identity and three comparison tables: NEURON ALIGNMENT decomposes the [[feature-direction]] into the 512 MLP neurons ([[neuron-basis-coefficients]]); CORRELATED NEURONS ranks neurons by how well their activations track the feature's ([[most-correlated-neuron]]); CORRELATED B FEATURES runs the same comparison against a dictionary trained on [[transformer-a-and-b|a second transformer differing only in seed]], which is [[universality]] measured by [[activation-similarity]].

Second column, two histograms. The upper one has [[feature-activation]] on $x$ — a ReLU output, so non-negative — and counts of sampled tokens on $y$, with exact zeros dropped and the firing rate quoted separately as [[feature-density]]. The lower one plots logit weights over the whole vocabulary, centred because softmax is shift-invariant, with ten tokens from each tail listed above it.

Third column, the [[top-dataset-examples|top 20 activating examples]]. Fourth, [[activation-interval|subsample intervals]] stepping down from the maximum, which is where an interpretation tends to fail.

Colour carries two channels at once. Orange background is activation strength on that token; underline colour is [[feature-ablation|ablation effect]] — blue where deleting the feature raised the loss, red where it lowered it ([[ablation-effect-visualization]]). Look at CORRELATED NEURONS first, then the intervals — not the top examples.

The search strip reads left to right as one query: a match mode, the field matched against (examples, logits, index, or the [[automated-interpretability|machine-written explanation]]), a sort key over all features, and Underline Mode, which chooses whether the underlines mean one feature ablated or the whole MLP replaced by the reconstruction ([[loss-recovered-by-features]]).

### What a bad result would look like

On the page shown, the strongest correlated neuron reaches only $+0.09$ while the best matching B-run feature reaches $+0.75$. Flip either and the page collapses. A correlated neuron at $0.9$ would mean [[dictionary-learning]] handed back a neuron under a new name. A best B feature at $0.1$ would mean the feature is an artifact of one seed. Coherent top examples above interval bands that read as noise would mean the interpretation holds only at the top of the range. A logit histogram with no tails would mean the feature does nothing downstream.

The page does not hide its weak spots: the human label reads `Latin: ?`, and the automated score is $0.305$ ([[activation-prediction-scoring]]) — above zero, far from a match.

### Where it comes back

As a whole shape, only twice: fig-4 and fig-5. Its panels return separately — activation histograms, logit tails, neuron-correlation tables, shaded text — through the case studies of Section 3. What changes between the two figures is that one carries evidence and the other carries none; what changes between browser pages is the run, so the same layout on a wider dictionary shows [[feature-splitting]] instead of one feature.

concepts.name: Feature-density histogram of a dictionary
concepts.summary: A log-scale histogram counting every feature in one trained autoencoder by how often it fires, typically splitting into an ultralow-density mode the paper discards as a training artifact and a bulk mode it keeps. It is the paper's quick per-run health check, read for its shape and its left edge rather than for any individual feature.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The paper says outright that it has no test-loss equivalent for [[dictionary-learning]] — nothing cheap to watch that tracks what it wants, interpretable features ([[evaluating-dictionary-learning]]). What it settles for is [[feature-density]]: the fraction of tokens on which a learned [[feature]] has a nonzero activation. Two things are wanted from a run — how many usable features came out, and how rare the rarest recovered one is.

Neither survives being averaged. The densities in a run are not one population but two, and a mean lands in the gap between them, describing no feature in either. A count of live features counts the junk as live: units firing on one token in ten million pass any zero-activity test. A bar chart with one height per run says nothing about where the left edge sits — and that edge is what the appendix's scaling argument rests on. The histogram is the smallest shape carrying both.

The log axis is forced too: the busiest features fire on well under 1% of tokens and the rarest around $10^{-7}$, so a linear axis would stack five orders of magnitude against the origin.

### How to read it, step by step

One chart covers one [[dictionary-learning-run]]: a single trained [[sparse-autoencoder]], named in the paper's run notation ([[feature-notation]]). Every hidden unit of it contributes one count to one bin, so this is a census, not a picture of any one feature.

The x axis is $\log_{10}$ of density. A tick at $-7$ is one token in ten million, $-5$ one in a hundred thousand, $-2$ one in a hundred. The y axis is a raw count of features per bin, not normalised by dictionary width — so in an overlay a wider run is taller for free, and height alone is not the evidence.

Units that never fire have density exactly $0$, which has no logarithm: [[dead-neurons]] are absent from the chart, not sitting at its left edge.

Look at the left edge first, then for a valley. The narrow spike near $10^{-7}$ is the [[ultralow-density-cluster]], which the paper reports is almost never interpretable and reads as a training artifact rather than anything in the transformer — [[de-facto-dead-neurons]]. The broad mass to its right is the [[high-density-cluster]], anecdotally almost all interpretable, the name comparative only. Colour differs by instance: in the single-run charts it hand-marks the bars the authors assign to the ultralow cluster; in the grid it encodes dictionary width.

### What a bad result would look like

For the diagnostic use: no valley. One smooth mound, nowhere to cut, and the run's usable feature count cannot be read off at all — a failure the paper itself puts on the page. For the sparsity check: a substantial pile of features above $10^{-2}$, which the paper's own checklist ([[feature-density-diagnostics]]) treats as the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]] being too weak.

For the scaling claim: curves growing taller as the dictionary widens while their left edge stays put. That would mean extra capacity going to duplicates of features already found — the signature of having exhausted the model's [[true-features]]. The paper's hedge is fair: more mass in the rare tail cannot, by counting alone, distinguish a genuinely new feature from [[feature-splitting]] of an old one.

### Where it comes back

Fig-64 is the clean case, run A/16, two modes separated and the left one labelled. Fig-65 is the same shape for A/5, the widest run at $131{,}072$ units, where the modes run together and the diagnostic stops working; the paper reports overlap as coming with large width and a large [[l1-coefficient]] $\lambda$, anecdotally and with no threshold. Its fallback is [[density-cluster-separation]] — add each feature's bias and its encoder-decoder dot product and the clusters pull apart in three dimensions.

Fig-67 stacks the shape into a grid: five panels of $\lambda$, six curves of dictionary width each, $512$ up to $131{,}072$ ([[expansion-factor]] $1\times$ to $256\times$). Read within a panel for the left edge marching left; across panels, for the whole distribution sliding left as the penalty rises. A reader who learned only "look for two humps" will over-read the two strongest-penalty panels, where the tall spikes are exactly the overlapping case.

concepts.name: Feature direction in the neuron basis (stem plot)
concepts.summary: One learned feature's decoder column drawn coordinate by coordinate, one stem per MLP neuron. It exists to answer a single question: is this feature one neuron under a new name, or is it spread across many?
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Section 3.1.4 asks a negative question: did [[dictionary-learning]] find something the neuron basis did not already contain, or did it hand back a well-behaved neuron under a new name? That check is [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]], and what settles it is a count — how many coordinates are large — not a ranking of which ones.

That rules out the usual displays. A bar chart of the ten biggest contributing neurons names the loudest players and throws the count away, which is the whole argument. A summary statistic — mean absolute coefficient, an effective-dimension score — takes similar values for a spike and a spread, so it separates nothing. A 512-row table is unreadable, and trimming it to the top rows assumes the answer. The stem plot is the bar chart that refuses to select: every coordinate gets a mark at its true height, so the flat majority and the loud minority sit together.

Sign is the second reason. Magnitude-sorted and absolute-value displays lose it, and here the three largest coefficients are negative — invisible to any search for neurons that light up on the target context, which is the other search the paper ran ([[top-dataset-example-search]]).

### How to read it, step by step

One stem is one MLP neuron of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]], which has 512 of them. The x axis, *Dictionary Vector Index*, is that neuron's index and nothing more. The ordering is arbitrary, so left-versus-right carries no information and there is no trend to read.

The y axis, *Weight Value*, is that neuron's entry in one column of the [[dictionary-decoder]] — the [[feature-direction]] the [[sparse-autoencoder]] writes along when the feature fires. These are [[neuron-basis-coefficients]]: read a stem as how much of that neuron's activation the feature adds when it is on, not as how strongly the neuron responds to the feature's context. Colour only restates the sign. Because MLP activations are non-negative, a red stem means the feature pushes that neuron down.

The scale is the part that misleads. Decoder columns are held at [[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]], so the 512 squared coefficients sum to $1$. That fixes two reference marks. A feature that *is* a neuron shows one stem at $\pm 1$ and 511 flat. A feature spread perfectly evenly shows every stem at $1/\sqrt{512} \approx 0.044$. So $0.044$ is the yardstick for "large", not $1.0$, and the paper's counting threshold of $0.1$ is a little over twice it — a chosen cutoff, not a derived one.

Look first at the zero line and judge what fraction of the 512 sits on it. Then count the stems past $0.1$. Then check the sign of the tallest few; individual neurons come last.

### What a bad result would look like

The falsifying picture is easy to draw: one stem near $0.9$, the rest flat. That would say the autoencoder relabelled a neuron, and for this feature the [[polysemanticity]] problem was never there. A softer failure is three or four stems near $0.5$ and nothing else — a feature in a small neuron subspace, which neuron-first analysis could still have found. The opposite failure is a flat comb at $0.044$ with no heavy tail, which would weaken the [[privileged-basis]] claim by making the neuron basis look like any random rotation.

One story this plot cannot exclude, and the paper says so: the coefficients might cancel so as to sharpen one neuron. That is why the argument moves on to the [[most-correlated-neuron]] over roughly 40 million examples.

### Where it comes back

Inside the paper's own case studies it does not — this is the only stem plot. The DNA section uses the quantity in prose without drawing it, naming the highest-coefficient neuron and noting it has no DNA in its top examples; the base64 and Hebrew sections switch to correlation scatter plots. The shape returns in bulk in the [[external-replication]], where each feature's coefficients are squared and ranked so that one dot stands for a whole vector: 92% of features come out spread rather than concentrated, alongside a [[kurtosis-privileged-basis-test]] that no single vector could support. Both are pictures of what [[superposition]] predicts, and of why some features end up [[features-invisible-in-the-neuron-basis]].

concepts.name: Feature relationship graph
concepts.summary: Features drawn as boxes, with labelled edges standing for a relation between them: either a handoff, where the tokens one feature promotes are the tokens the next one fires on, or a similarity link between features in dictionaries of different widths. It is for claims that live between features rather than inside any one of them.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Two of the paper's claims are about *relations between* features, and neither survives being written one feature at a time.

The first: some [[feature]]s hand off to each other through generated text — the tokens one promotes are the tokens the next fires on ([[finite-state-automata-features]]). The evidence is a coincidence between two lists — a feature's top predicted tokens, another's firing set — which only reads as evidence with both adjacent. A table hides it: you would do the matching yourself and never see the chain close into a cycle.

The second: [[feature-splitting]] across dictionary widths, where the paper argues refinement is not a tree — features at one size both split and merge into the next ([[splitting-is-not-a-tree]]). A dendrogram forbids that by construction; a table buries the one node with two parents. And there is no specificity score to bar-chart: "more specific" is read off human descriptions, which therefore have to be on the page for the reader to check.

### How to read it, step by step

No axes; position is layout. One exception: the splitting graph's horizontal is an ordered sweep of [[dictionary-learning-run]]s — $512$, $4{,}096$, $16{,}384$ features, same transformer, only width changing.

A node is one feature: a direction in the 512-dimensional MLP activation space recovered by the [[sparse-autoencoder]], named model / run / index ([[feature-notation]]), the index arbitrary. What fills it is evidence: in the automaton figures a strip of [[top-dataset-examples]] with orange marking the [[feature-activation]] per token, darker for stronger ([[activation-visualization-sampling]]); in the splitting graph, a human description.

The edges are the trap. In the automaton figures an arrow is not a weight, a wire, or a circuit. Its label lists the source's largest positive [[logit-weight]] entries — the tokens it pushes hardest in the next-token distribution — and points at the feature those tokens switch on. The handoff travels through emitted text, one token later; nothing inside the model joins the two. So read an arrow's token list, then the orange tokens in the box it points at: the same tokens? If so the arrow is earned. Then check whether you return where you started. A dashed arrow exits the diagram: a predicted token no node accounts for.

In the splitting graph an edge means only that a [[masked-cosine-similarity]] cleared a threshold: cosine between two features' activations over the tokens where the first fires, again over those where the second fires, keep the larger, line drawn above about $0.4$. The paper says it was chosen for display. Colour marks which coarse feature a branch descends from, nothing else.

### What a bad result would look like

For the automata: arrows whose labelled tokens are not the tokens the target box highlights. Or no cycle. Or labels made of high-frequency tokens any feature would promote, making the handoff a fact about token statistics.

Nothing here is an intervention. Both ends of every arrow are truncated top-$k$ lists from the interface: no ablation, no measure that emitting the token raises the target's activation. The tidiness is also resolution-dependent: A/0 has 512 features for a 512-dimensional space, so it is not overcomplete ([[overcompleteness]]), and the paper says wider runs split each node and complicate the system.

For the splitting graph: children as broad as their parents, or wandering off the parent's subject. Or threshold sensitivity — lower it enough and everything links to everything; no sweep is shown. The one corroboration beyond descriptions is downstream: the coarse "the in mathematical prose" feature promotes generic tokens (*the theorem*), its fine descendants topical ones (*the classifier*).

### Where it comes back

Fig-58 is the reference case: four A/0 features cycling open bracket, tag name, tag close, newline-and-indent, back to open bracket ([[html-feature-automaton]]). Fig-57 runs the shape twice on Unicode, where a character arrives as a prefix byte plus a suffix byte ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]): Tamil is a clean two-node cycle, Chinese adds a self-loop because a complete single-token character sits where a suffix would ([[unicode-token-state-machines]]).

Fig-46 keeps the boxes and changes what an edge means entirely — and pulls the opposite way: the automata are legible because A/0 is coarse, while the splitting graph shows what happens when you stop being coarse.

concepts.name: Features-versus-neurons score histogram
concepts.summary: Two populations of units — the autoencoder's learned features and the transformer's own MLP neurons — scored on one number and drawn as overlapping histograms on a shared axis. It is how the paper argues at population scale, rather than by example, that its features are more interpretable and more reproducible than neurons.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The paper's case is comparative: it claims the directions its [[sparse-autoencoder|sparse autoencoder]] learns are more interpretable than the MLP neurons already in the model. Elsewhere it argues that one feature at a time, which invites the charge of [[cherry-picked-case-studies|cherry-picking]]. The histogram is the same claim at population scale — every scored unit is in the picture.

Given one number per unit, a mean or a two-row table is the obvious move, and it would hide what the paper most wants shown. In the hand-scored figure neurons average 3.2 but their *median* is 0: an average suggests a mediocre middle, when most neurons scored nothing at all and a thin minority scored well. A distribution also shows whether the gap is a whole population shifted or a tail doing the work. Overlaying both on one axis makes separation, or its absence, the visible fact.

### How to read it, step by step

The horizontal axis is one score, computed once per unit, and a "unit" is either one autoencoder [[feature]] (one dictionary direction) or one MLP neuron of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed|one-layer model]]. Which score changes by figure: a 0–14 rubric total, a [[spearman-correlation]] between predicted and true activations, a yes/no accuracy, a [[pearson-correlation]] to the nearest match in a second model.

The vertical axis is usually **density**, not count: each population is separately normalised to enclose area 1. The populations are unequal — about 3,676 features against 512 neurons — so raw counts would erase the neurons. It also means bar height says nothing about how many units were scored. To convert, multiply height by bin width: height $4$ over bins of width $0.02$ is about $8\%$ of that population. Only the hand-scored figure uses Count, where the samples are small and similar in size.

Crimson is features, teal is neurons, yellow where a third population (the [[randomized-transformer]] baseline) appears. Dark navy is the two translucent fills lying on top of each other — overlap, not a third group. That is the trap the chart sets, and navy area is exactly the evidence *against* the claim.

Look first at the two small triangles under the axis: those are the medians, and the distance between them is the claim. Then the dotted "random chance" line, if there is one, and whether the teal mode sits on it. Then the legend chips, which repeat median and mean and give a "failures" count — runs where the scoring model replied in a format the harness could not parse, so the unit was dropped rather than scored badly. Those describe the pipeline, not the units. Never read a claim off one bar.

### What a bad result would look like

Two histograms lying on each other: mostly navy, one shared mode, the triangles nearly touching. That would say the learned directions are no easier to explain than the neurons the model came with — that [[dictionary-learning]] bought nothing. Weaker failures count too: crimson beating teal on the mean while both share a mode, so the typical feature is no better and a tail carries the average; or teal already well above chance, undercutting the [[polysemanticity|polysemantic-neuron]] premise that motivated the approach. The importance-weighted figure comes close to the first bad picture, and the paper says so rather than burying it.

### Where it comes back

Fig-39 is the human arm: a [[feature-interpretability-rubric|rubric]] total from a [[blinded-annotation|blinded]] rater, counts rather than density, medians 12 against 0. Fig-40 and fig-41 are the two [[automated-interpretability]] arms — activation prediction (0.58 against 0.2, with a teal spike at exactly zero that is a scoring artifact) and [[automated-logit-scoring|logit-weight prediction]] against a 0.5 chance line (0.73 against 0.53). Fig-52 reuses the shape for a different question, [[universality]]: the axis is agreement with the closest match in an independently trained model, medians 0.72 against 0.46, with example cards pinned to points on the axis. Fig-71 replots fig-40's score after [[importance-scoring]] reweights the sampling, and both populations slump toward zero. Fig-72 is the odd one out: three populations in stacked rows rather than overlaid, and its axis is explanation length, not a score — a caveat check whose good outcome is three rows that look alike.

concepts.name: Score across the activation spectrum
concepts.summary: A line chart that scores how well a unit's interpretation holds at each band of its own activation range, from its weakest firings to its maximum, with autoencoder features and raw MLP neurons on the same axes. It exists to test whether interpretability survives outside the top-activating examples.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The paper's headline interpretability result — [[manual-interpretability-scoring|a blinded human scoring features against neurons]] — is one number per unit. That format cannot answer the question this section raises: does the interpretation the annotator settled on hold everywhere the unit fires, or only where it fires hardest? The worry is specific. The standard way to read a unit is to collect its top-activating dataset examples, and the paper admits that method flatters [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]] units, which often look clean at their maximum and messy further down ([[max-dataset-example-bias|the maximal-example weakness]]). Any summary that averages over a unit's whole range — a bar chart, a mean, a histogram of totals — folds that failure mode back in and hides it.

So the spectrum has to become an axis. A table of per-band means for 162 units would carry the numbers but not the shape, and the claim here is about shape: interpretability should rise with activation strength, and the reader needs to see where it rises, how steeply, and how far the two series stay apart. Plotting [[feature|features]] and neurons on the same axes also exposes something a features-only plot would not — neurons improve with activation strength too, so the rise is a property of firing hard, not a property of the dictionary.

### How to read it, step by step

The x axis is the [[activation-interval|activation interval]]: each unit's range from zero to its own maximum, cut into eleven evenly spaced bands, with examples sampled uniformly from each. The labels `~0%` through `~100%` are fractions of that unit's own peak, so `~50%` means half of *this* unit's maximum and never an absolute activation. That normalisation is what lets a feature whose max is 9 and one whose max is 0.6 share a column.

The y axis is a single line item of the [[feature-interpretability-rubric|interpretability rubric]], scored 0 to 5. The annotator commits to one interpretation of the whole unit first, then rates each band on how consistent that band's strongly-firing tokens are with it. A low score therefore does not mean the band is confusing on its own — it means the band disagrees with the one story the annotator committed to.

Colour is the unit type: magenta for [[sparse-autoencoder|autoencoder]] features, teal for the transformer's own [[neuron-notation|MLP neurons]], both scored [[blinded-annotation|without the annotator knowing which was which]]. The faded dots are individual scored intervals, pinned to integer heights, darker where more of them stacked up. The lines are per-band averages over those dots — roughly 37 intervals per band, so small wobbles are noise.

Look first at the dotted line at 3, then at where each curve meets it. The label calls it a *subjective* threshold; it is the authors' impression, not a derived cutoff.

### What a bad result would look like

The clearest failure would be a magenta line running along the teal one — [[dictionary-learning]] buying no interpretability the neuron basis did not already have. The subtler and more interesting failure is a magenta line near 5 in the top band that collapses by the `~60%` band: that would say features look [[monosemanticity|monosemantic]] only through the very lens this analysis was built to distrust.

Neither happens, but neither does the strong result. A magenta line above 3 in every band, including `~0%`, would mean the interpretation covers the whole range; instead it starts near 2.6 and crosses around `~20%`. The paper does not explain that low end, offering only that a direction learned [[feature-at-slight-angle|at a slight angle]] to the true one would misbehave there.

Two cautions the chart invites. Move the threshold to 4 and the crossing slides to `~40%`; the gap between the curves is sturdier evidence than the crossing point. And check the dot cloud — a mean of 2.6 drawn from scores split between 5 and 0 would describe no unit at all.

### Where it comes back

This exact shape is used once. Its pieces recur. Read it against the rubric histogram, which is the same annotator and the same scoring collapsed to one total per unit: that plot sizes the feature–neuron gap, this one says where along the spectrum the gap lives. The per-feature activation-distribution plots in the case studies ask the same question with a [[computational-proxy|computational proxy]] instead of a human, colouring an absolute activation axis by how likely the context is under the hypothesis — and they show the same drift, purer at the top of the range than the bottom. The [[automated-interpretability|automated-interpretability]] plots swap the human for a language model but report distributions, not bands.

That soft low end is the admitted weak point: [[low-interval-activation-skew|most activations are small]], so most of them land in the worst-scoring bands. The paper's defence is that [[large-activations-dominate|the large activations carry most of the effect]] on the model's output.

concepts.name: Logit-weight histogram over the vocabulary
concepts.summary: A histogram of one unit's logit weights, one number per vocabulary entry saying how much that token's next-token logit moves when the unit fires, with each column coloured by an independent score for whether the token belongs to the hypothesised context. It is the paper's first check that a feature does what it fires on, and the claim lives in the small second mode out in the right tail, not in the towering mode at zero.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

[[dictionary-learning]] here is fit to MLP activations and nothing else, so a sceptic can say the [[feature|features]] are structure in the training data, not in the model. The reply is to ask what the next-token distribution does when a unit fires ([[feature-downstream-effects]]) — a check independent of how the feature was found, since logits never enter the autoencoder's objective ([[downstream-effects-outside-dictionary-learning]]).

One number per vocabulary entry means tens of thousands of them, so a bar chart is out. So is an average: softmax is shift-invariant, the weights have no absolute zero, and the paper slides each unit's until the median is $0$ ([[logit-weight-median-centering]]), leaving any mean near zero by construction. The obvious alternative, a table of the twenty highest-weighted tokens, hides the claim — which is not "the top tokens are Arabic" but "the vocabulary splits": a bulk the unit barely touches, and a small coherent group far away that it pushes hard. A table cannot say whether its twentieth row sits above the bulk or inside it.

### How to read it, step by step

This looks like the activation histogram ([[feature-activation-distribution-plot]]) — same blue-to-red legend, same strip under the axis — but it counts something else. There, one observation was one token of sampled text; here it is one vocabulary entry, and no text is run at all. It says what a unit writes, never when it fires.

The x axis is the [[logit-weight]], $-0.6$ to $0.6$: push the [[feature-direction]] through the [[mlp-output-weights]], a [[layer-norm-linearization|linearised layer norm]] and the [[unembedding-matrix]] ($d_i W_{down} \pi L W_{unembed}$, the [[path-expansion-logit-attribution]]) to get how much one unit of activation adds to that token's next-token logit. The y axis is density in vocabulary entries per unit of weight, so area is a count and peaks run to $0.2$–$0.4$M over an axis $1.2$ wide. Extremely rare or never-used entries are dropped ([[anomalous-token-exclusion]]). Colour comes from outside the histogram: each token string is scored by a [[computational-proxy]], the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log(P(s\mid H)/P(s))$ clipped to $\pm 5$, and each column is stacked by that score.

Do not look first at the tall mode at zero. It is nearly the whole vocabulary, and the paper's label on it is "Interference Weights?", question mark included — a guess that this is cross-talk forced by [[superposition]] rather than anything the model uses ([[weight-interference]]). The result is the [[logit-weight-second-mode]] in the right tail, near $0.3$–$0.5$ and small enough to need an inset. Read the strip to find where the colour turns, then the inset to confirm there is mass there.

### What a bad result would look like

One mode, no separated bump, and the red tokens scattered through the bulk on both sides of zero. The paper draws that version itself: A/neuron/489, the [[most-correlated-neuron]] to the Arabic feature, spreads its Arabic tokens from about $-0.25$ to $+0.32$, "very slightly positive leaning overall, but some are negative" (fig-15). The other failure is a second mode of the wrong tokens: A/neuron/470 has one, and it holds 'htm', 'png', 'pdf' — filename endings, not base64 (fig-31). Both are read as [[feature-neuron-nonalignment]], consistent with [[polysemanticity]].

Two things the shape cannot settle, and the paper says so ([[logit-weight-caveats]]): the weights may be too small to matter once multiplied by real activations, and the unit may only fire where other features already rule those tokens out. Hence [[feature-ablation]] and [[pinned-feature-sampling]] alongside. Note too that the strip renormalises every column, so a few tokens can paint a solid red band; check density first.

### Where it comes back

Four case studies: fig-10 (Arabic), fig-22 (DNA), fig-26 (base64), fig-34 (Hebrew). What changes is the hypothesis, its proxy, and how sharp the handover is. Arabic and Hebrew flip almost as a step, helped by each script concentrating on one lead byte — \xd8/\xd9, \xd7 ([[utf8-multi-token-characters]]). Base64 slides instead: 'fr' is both a French abbreviation and a legal base64 pair, which is why fig-26's caption points at the strip rather than the histogram.

Three repeat the plot for the matched feature in the second transformer: fig-18, fig-28, fig-37. Those features were selected by activation correlation alone, so a matching second mode is separate evidence for [[universality]]. Two are the neuron controls, fig-15 and fig-31.

concepts.name: Scoring-robustness panel grid
concepts.summary: A grid of histograms crossing several invented interpretability scores against several populations of units — dictionary-learning features, MLP neurons, and features from a randomized transformer. It exists to show that the feature-over-neuron ordering survives every scoring choice, so no single panel is the result.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

Every interpretability score in this paper is something the paper made up. There is no ground truth for "is this unit interpretable", so the paper builds several imperfect graders — a blinded human [[feature-interpretability-rubric]], [[automated-interpretability]] on activations, the same explanation checked against output weights — and none of them is trusted on its own. The claim being defended is not a number; it is an *ordering*: [[dictionary-learning]] [[feature|features]] are more interpretable than the transformer's own MLP neurons, which are expected to be [[polysemanticity|polysemantic]]. A single bar chart of medians would state that ordering but leave open the obvious reply — that it holds only for the grader you chose. So one axis of the grid varies the scoring method and the other varies the population being scored, and the finding is that the ordering survives the crossing.

A plain average would also have hidden the shapes, which here carry the argument. These distributions are skewed, spiky and sometimes bimodal: a tall column sitting exactly on zero correlation, because a constant prediction has no defined correlation and gets scored zero ([[constant-prediction-zero-score]]); a second clump at the far right. A mean over that is meaningless, which is why the paper marks medians with triangles and plots the full histogram behind them.

### How to read it, step by step

In fig-69, rows are scoring methods and columns are populations. The three columns are fixed all the way down: run A/1 features ([[feature-notation]]), the MLP neurons of that same transformer, and features from a [[randomized-transformer]] whose weight matrices had their entries shuffled in place ([[weight-shuffling]]). Row 1 is the human rubric, $0$–$14$, plotted as raw counts because the human sample is small — a few hundred scored [[activation-interval|activation intervals]], not units. Rows 2 and 3 are the *same* automated experiment scored twice, once with [[pearson-correlation]] and once with [[spearman-correlation]]; row 4 is [[automated-logit-scoring]], an accuracy where $0.5$ is chance. Rows 2–4 plot density, so panels with different unit counts are comparable. The dotted vertical line is the null value for that row.

Look first down a column, then across. Down: does this population's shape hold under all four graders? Across: within one grader, does the left column beat the middle? Rows 2 and 3 should be read against each other directly — they differ only in the coefficient, and if the shapes track, the choice of coefficient did not make the result.

Fig-70 keeps the shape but rotates it. Population becomes colour — magenta for A/1, yellow for randomized, dark orange where they overlap — and the panels become the three scores.

### What a bad result would look like

The ordering flipping between rows 2 and 3, or holding under the automated graders but not the human one. Or medians that separate while the histograms sit almost entirely on top of each other, so the gap is a summary statistic and not a difference. Or the randomized column tracking the feature column everywhere, which would mean the decomposition recovers dataset regularities rather than anything the model computes ([[model-vs-data-question]]).

One cell does go the wrong way, and the paper leaves it in and labels it. On the activation score the randomized features take the higher median — roughly $0.62$ against $0.57$. This is the cell readers lift out and quote. The paper's answer is that the randomized model has more, and more strictly, [[single-token-features]], which are trivial to explain and so trivial to score; splitting the panel on that property reverses the ordering ([[randomized-feature-bimodality]]). Note that this split is chosen after seeing the awkward result, and the paper's further claim — that the remaining randomized features are uninterpretable — rests partly on the authors reporting they could not construct sensible interpretations, and inviting readers to check.

### Where it comes back

Fig-69 is the full four-by-three crossing, run to show the Pearson/Spearman choice does not matter. Fig-70 narrows to the two populations and the one cell that misbehaves, adding the single-token split as an inset. The importance-weighted rescoring then reruns the same populations under yet another correction to the grader — the same move, one more time.

concepts.name: Sparsity against explained behaviour
concepts.summary: A scatter in which every dot is one trained sparse autoencoder, placed by how few features fire per token against how much of the MLP layer's loss contribution its reconstruction recovers. It is for pricing a hyperparameter choice: what a looser sparsity penalty, or a wider dictionary, actually buys.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The paper reports finding no single number that says whether [[dictionary-learning]] is working, so it triangulates from several imperfect proxies ([[evaluating-dictionary-learning]]). Two of those proxies pull against each other. The [[l0-norm]] — the mean count of features with a nonzero activation on a token — rewards a code where almost nothing fires. The share of the MLP layer's loss contribution the reconstruction recovers ([[loss-recovered-by-features]]) rewards a code that reproduces the layer. Either alone is gameable: rank the runs in a bar chart by explained loss and the densest dictionary wins; rank by sparsity and the emptiest does. A table of chosen hyperparameters, or an average, hides that "best" is undefined until you say what a unit of sparsity is worth — and a dictionary firing two hundred features per token explains plenty while being no easier to read than the 512 neurons it replaced.

Carrying both numbers on one dot lets a reader price a gain rather than rank it, which is as far as the appendix goes: no derived optimum, only a stated habit of targeting $L^0$ below 10 or 20 and distrusting codes whose $L^0$ is a large fraction of the layer's 512 dimensions ([[l0-nll-tradeoff]]).

### How to read it, step by step

The horizontal axis is average $L^0$: a plain count of active features per token, linear, running from about 4 to 20. Left is sparser. The vertical axis, 0.67 to about 0.95, comes from splicing the reconstruction in place of the real MLP activations, measuring how much the loss rises, dividing by the rise from zeroing the layer outright ([[zero-ablation-baseline]]), and subtracting from one. It is labelled "Percent" but ticked in fractions, so 0.95 means 95%.

One dot is not a feature. It is an entire trained [[sparse-autoencoder]] — one [[dictionary-learning-run]], its width and penalty fixed, against the same one-layer transformer. Colour encodes the [[l1-coefficient]] $\lambda$ on the [[l1-sparsity-penalty]]: 0.004 blue, 0.006 red, 0.008 green, 0.01 purple. Each line joins six dictionary sizes ([[expansion-factor]]), 512 up to 131,072; it is a connector, not a fit.

Look first at the horizontal gaps between colours, not along any one curve. The penalty fixes which vertical band a run lands in — purple near 4 to 7 active features, blue near 16 to 20 — and the bands barely overlap. Then look upward inside a band: a 256-fold wider dictionary climbs purple from about 0.67 to 0.89 while $L^0$ shifts by under three. Two knobs, two directions. Blue's best point, 0.945, buys about 1.5 points over red's 0.93 for roughly double the active features.

### What a bad result would look like

If the four colours lay strung along one shared curve, penalty and width would be the same lever and the two-knob reading would be wrong. If each line ran flat, width would buy nothing and the recovered fraction would belong to $\lambda$ alone. If the bands overlapped — some run at $L^0 \approx 5$ matching the best run at $L^0 \approx 20$ — there would be no tradeoff to read, only a dominated region and an obvious pick.

The soft spots matter too. The paper calls the percentage an overestimate, because zero-ablating the MLP may be an unusually bad baseline ([[reconstructed-nll-overestimate-caveat]]), and says without showing data that a small-MLP transformer trained from scratch reaches similar numbers. The $\lambda = 0.001$ runs are dropped to keep the scale readable, cropping out the dense end. And the paper expects a long tail of features, each later percentage point needing more of them, so climbing a band is not closing in on a complete account.

### Where it comes back

This pairing of axes appears once, in the hyperparameter appendix. The y-axis number returns bare in the section on how much of the model the interpretation explains: 79% for A/1, 94.5% for A/5 — two of these blue dots, quoted without the tradeoff around them. The same sweep grid is shown a second way as [[feature-density]] histograms grouped by L1 coefficient ([[feature-density-histogram]]), where widening the dictionary turns up rarer features rather than more explained loss, and a third way in [[feature-splitting]], where that same widening makes one feature divide into a family.

concepts.name: UMAP map of dictionary directions
concepts.summary: A scatter of every learned feature's decoder direction, projected to two dimensions so that nearby dots mean small angles between dictionary vectors. It is for seeing whether feature families found by reading text are also geometric clumps, and whether coarse features sit inside the finer ones that split out of them.
concepts.explanation:
### Why this chart and not another

The paper arrives at feature splitting with families it found by reading text: several base64 features, several Arabic script features, over a hundred features for the token "the" in different contexts. Those families were assembled by a human looking at activating dataset examples. The question that forces this chart is whether they are anything more than a habit of the reader — whether the [[sparse-autoencoder]] happened to place conceptually similar features in similar places in activation space, without ever being asked to.

A single number would not settle it. Mean within-family cosine similarity against mean across-family similarity presupposes the families, so it can only confirm the ones already named; it hides the clusters nobody labelled, and it says nothing about how many groups there are or whether they are separate. A table of pairwise similarities is 4,608 rows by 4,608 columns in the smaller case. A bar chart needs its categories fixed in advance. The authors want the opposite: to look at the geometry with the labels off and see whether structure shows up on its own. A projected scatter is the cheapest way to do that, and the price is two axes that carry no information at all.

The second job is [[feature-splitting]], which needs coarse and fine dictionaries in one coordinate system — do the finer features a wider run splits out land where the coarse feature was? Separate maps per run cannot answer that, so every run goes into one embedding.

### How to read it, step by step

One dot is one [[feature-direction]]: a single column of the decoder matrix $W_d$ ([[dictionary-decoder]]), the direction a feature writes into the 512-dimensional MLP activation space of the [[one-layer-transformer-testbed]] when it fires. Not an activation, not a firing rate, not a strength. Columns are held at unit length ([[unit-norm-dictionary-columns]]), so all the information is in angles between them.

[[umap]] takes those 512 numbers down to two, with cosine as the distance metric (`n_neighbors=15`; `min_dist=0.05` in fig-1, `0.01` in fig-44). Both axes are UMAP output coordinates — no units, no scale, no fixed orientation, and no meaning if you rerun the fit. What the method tries to preserve is which points were neighbours. So read co-location and nothing else: the width of a gap between two blobs is not a distance, and a point's position on its own says nothing.

Colour encodes the [[dictionary-learning-run]]. In fig-44 the large grey markers are A/0 (512 features, 1x [[expansion-factor]]), dark green is A/1 (4,096, 8x), small light green is A/2 (16,384, 32x) — same transformer, same sparsity coefficient, only dictionary width changing.

Look first at a labelled knot. Arabic script, base64: check that it holds all three colours, with one oversized grey marker sitting as a halo under a spray of green. That halo is what splitting looks like geometrically. Then look at the island set far apart on the right: [[ultralow-density-cluster]] features and [[dead-neurons]], which the paper treats as artifacts of autoencoder training rather than facts about the transformer.

### What a bad result would look like

If conceptually similar features had unrelated directions, the labelled families would be scattered: the Arabic features spread through the mass instead of forming one knot, and the clusters that do appear would cut across the human labels rather than agreeing with them. Random unit vectors in 512 dimensions are close to mutually orthogonal, so a dictionary carrying no such structure should project to one diffuse ball — roughly what the ultralow-density and dead region on the right already looks like, which is a useful sight to keep as the null picture.

If splitting were not happening, colour would organise the map instead of theme: grey A/0 points would occupy their own territory rather than sitting inside green knots, meaning the wider run had found different directions rather than finer versions of the same ones.

One weakness worth holding: UMAP will draw clusters out of almost any input, and the paper shows no shuffled or randomised control. The map corroborates the text-based families; on its own it does not prove them. The paper's stated claim is correspondingly modest — that the qualitative clusters are reflected in the dictionary's geometry ([[feature-geometry-clusters]]).

### Where it comes back

Two versions appear. Fig-1 is the interactive browser published with the article: A/0 and A/1 together, 4,608 points, all one colour, paired with a scrollable list of human-written labels grouped by [[hdbscan-feature-clustering]] — the labels sit beside the map so a reader can check that a clump really is thematic. Fig-44 drops the labels and adds A/2, then colours by run, which is the change that makes splitting legible. Same shape, two different questions: one asks whether clusters mean something, the other asks what happens to them as the dictionary grows.

concepts.name: Scaling laws for dictionary learning
concepts.summary: The wanted-but-missing relationships between subject model size and the autoencoder width and data needed to decompose it.
concepts.explanation: The authors state enormous uncertainty here and pose the questions directly: as the subject model gets bigger, does the ideal [[expansion-factor]] stay constant? How does the amount of data required change? They say the answers determine whether the approach can reach frontier models at all, and that they would ideally have scaling laws of the kind established for language model training.

citedFrom.refText: Kaplan, Jared et al. Scaling laws for neural language models. arXiv:2001.08361
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The template for the kind of empirical law being asked for; what such laws look like and what they predict is assumed known.

concepts.name: Handling Partial-Character Tokens
concepts.summary: When a token is not a complete Unicode character, its script is estimated empirically by sampling occurrences of it in the corpus.
concepts.explanation: Byte-level tokenization can produce tokens that are fragments of a multi-byte character, for which the Unicode block test is undefined. The paper handles these by sampling random occurrences of the token in the dataset and recording the fraction of the time it appears in a given script. This is the only part of the script proxy that is measured rather than assumed.

concepts.name: Unicode Block Detection
concepts.summary: Whether a character belongs to a script is decided by checking its Unicode block — for Arabic, ranges including U+0600–U+06FF and U+0750–U+077F.
concepts.explanation: The heuristic is a lookup: a character counts as Arabic if it falls in one of the Unicode blocks associated with Arabic script. The paper is explicit about the consequence: characters shared across languages, such as punctuation, count as non-Arabic, so a string of Arabic words containing a comma is scored as not entirely Arabic. Since $P(\text{Arabic}|s)$ collapses to $10^{-10}$ in that case, this interacts directly with the maximization over prefixes, which can find a punctuation-free suffix.

concepts.name: Adam and Decoder Normalization
concepts.summary: A fix for the mismatch created by renormalizing dictionary vectors after each step: project the gradient onto the sphere before the update rather than snapping back afterwards.
concepts.explanation: The naive way to enforce unit-norm dictionary vectors is to rescale them to length 1 after every gradient step. That silently discards whatever part of the update pointed along the vector, so the gradient Adam thinks it applied differs from the one that actually took effect — and because Adam's moment estimates are built from those gradients, the error compounds through the optimizer state. The paper instead removes the component of the gradient parallel to each dictionary vector before the step, so the update Adam sees is the update that happens. It reports a small but real reduction in total loss, and lists this last in its rough ordering of modifications by importance.

citedFrom.refText: Kingma, Diederik P and Ba, Jimmy. Adam: A method for stochastic optimization. arXiv:1412.6980
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The fix and the resampling state-reset both turn on how Adam's per-parameter moment estimates accumulate; the mechanism is in the Adam paper.
