Interaction Between Adam and Decoder Normalization

concepts.name: Algorithmic alternatives to the plain L1 autoencoder
concepts.summary: Candidate refinements listed as future work: variational autoencoders, sparsity priors beyond L1, and noise injection.
concepts.explanation: The authors suggest sparse-coding variational autoencoders, and regularization schemes that promote sparsity in ways an L1 penalty on activations cannot — for example encouraging sparsity in the interactions between features in different layers rather than in the activations themselves. They also note prior findings that injecting noise increases neuron interpretability by a route separate from an L1 penalty. None of these is tried in the paper.

concepts.name: Encoder as Amortized Sparse Coding
concepts.summary: The framing that the encoder is a single-shot linear stand-in for a multi-step, non-linear sparse coding algorithm.
concepts.explanation: Classical sparse coding solves an optimization problem separately for each datapoint to find its coefficients. The autoencoder instead learns one linear map, applied identically to every input, that approximates the answer that optimization would give — an amortized approximation, paid for once at training time rather than per datapoint. The paper uses this framing twice: to explain why the encoder should be allowed weights independent of the decoder (an amortized approximator has no reason to be the decoder's transpose), and to argue that the autoencoder is not 'too strong' relative to what the model itself can compute. It also explains the asymmetry in the architecture — the decoder is the dictionary, the encoder is the inference procedure.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: Encoder
concepts.summary: The linear map plus bias plus ReLU that turns an activation vector into feature activations: $\mathbf{f} = \text{ReLU}(W_e\bar{\mathbf{x}} + \mathbf{b}_e)$.
concepts.explanation: The encoder is the part that solves the hard inner problem — inferring which features are on and how strongly, from a vector that is a superposition of many of them. Because it is a single linear layer followed by ReLU, it can only do this approximately, in one shot, for every input. The ReLU is what makes the feature activations non-negative and what allows most of them to be exactly zero on any given datapoint, which is what sparsity means here.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: Autoencoder Training Dataset
concepts.summary: Roughly 10 billion MLP activation vectors harvested from the transformer over 40 million Pile contexts, of which just over 8 billion are used.
concepts.explanation: To build the dataset, the paper runs the trained transformers over 40 million contexts from [[pile-dataset|the Pile]] and collects the MLP activation vector after the ReLU for every token. It then samples activations from 250 tokens in each context and shuffles them together so that samples within a batch come from diverse contexts. Training uses a batch size of 8192 and 1 million update steps, consuming just over 8 billion of the 10 billion collected vectors. The paper reports that dataset scale mattered: training on more data made features subjectively 'sharper' and more interpretable.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Dataset and Basic Training

concepts.name: Decoder as Dictionary
concepts.summary: The output weight matrix $W_d$, whose columns are the feature directions. The paper uses "decoder" and "dictionary" interchangeably.
concepts.explanation: Reconstruction is $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = W_d\mathbf{f} + \mathbf{b}_d$, so each column of $W_d$ is the direction in MLP activation space that a given feature writes along, scaled by that feature's activation. This makes the columns the $\mathbf{d}_i$ of the [[dictionary-learning]] formulation, and the paper refers to them as dictionary vectors throughout. When the paper needs a vector representation of a feature — for comparing features across runs or across transformers, or for the UMAP embeddings — it uses the feature's decoder column.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: Expansion factor
concepts.summary: The ratio of autoencoder hidden dimension to input dimension — how many times more features than neurons the dictionary has.
concepts.explanation: The paper trains autoencoders across this whole range on a 512-neuron MLP, and focuses detailed analysis on an 8× run with 4,096 features. Expansion factor is the knob that produces [[feature-splitting]]: as it grows, coarse features refine into families of more specific ones. It is also the parameter whose scaling behavior is most uncertain for larger models — the authors ask whether the ideal expansion factor stays constant as the subject model grows, and note that a 100× autoencoder on a width-10,000 MLP would have about 20 billion parameters.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

concepts.name: Training Past the Loss Plateau
concepts.summary: The paper keeps training well beyond the point where training loss appears flat, listing 'many training steps' among its important modifications.
concepts.explanation: The paper trains for 1 million update steps and says explicitly that this goes beyond when the training loss looks to have plateaued. It reports that continued training kills off more ultralow-density neurons, which it treats as cleanup rather than loss. The claim is that a flat loss curve is not a reliable signal that the dictionary has stopped improving in the ways that matter for interpretability — which is consistent with the paper's broader difficulty in finding any single metric that tracks what it cares about.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Dataset and Basic Training
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: External replication and commentary
concepts.summary: Invited outside researchers commented on the work before publication; one trained his own sparse autoencoder on a different open source one-layer model and reports the core results replicate.
concepts.explanation: The practice follows the original Circuits Thread and Distill's discussion-article experiment. The replication used the MLP layer of an open source one-layer GELU language model, and found a significant fraction of latent features interpretable, with case studies including a title case feature and an 'and I' feature. Two trained autoencoders, a tutorial, and a rough training codebase were open sourced alongside. The commentary also contributes the findings on decoder density, kurtosis, ultra-low frequency clusters, and weight tying.

concepts.name: Feature Notation
concepts.summary: The paper's identifier scheme: run seed, autoencoder size index, and feature index, as in A/1/3450 or B/1/1334; neurons are written A/neurons/489.
concepts.explanation: The first portion, A or B, says which transformer the feature came from. The second says which [[dictionary-learning-run]] — runs differ in the number of learned factors and the [[l1-coefficient]], and the paper keeps a table of all of them. The last portion picks out the individual feature within that run. This three-part address is necessary because 'the same' feature can appear differently across runs and across transformers, and the paper's arguments about splitting and universality are precisely about relating features with different addresses.

concepts.name: Kaiming Uniform Initialization
concepts.summary: The default PyTorch weight initialization used for the autoencoder.
concepts.explanation: The autoencoder's weights start from PyTorch's default Kaiming Uniform scheme, which draws weights from a uniform range scaled by fan-in so that activation variance is preserved through a ReLU layer. The paper states this only for reproducibility. It also appears as a baseline in the resampling comparison: reinitializing [[dead-neurons]] with plain Kaiming Uniform performed worse than the paper's data-seeded resampling.

citedFrom.refText: He, Kaiming and Zhang, Xiangyu and Ren, Shaoqing and Sun, Jian. Delving deep into rectifiers: Surpassing human-level performance on imagenet classification. ICCV
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The exact initialization distribution is a reproduction detail defined in the cited paper.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: L1 penalty on feature activations
concepts.summary: A penalty on the sum of feature activations, which pushes most of them to exactly zero. This is what buys sparsity in the decomposition.
concepts.explanation: The loss is L2 reconstruction error plus an L1 penalty on the hidden layer activations. Without the penalty, an overcomplete autoencoder could reconstruct perfectly using dense, meaningless codes; the penalty is what selects a sparse decomposition, matching the sparsity that superposition predicts. Because the reconstruction objective is MSE rather than cross-entropy, this sparsity pressure can genuinely inhibit superposition forming inside the dictionary — otherwise one would have superposition 'all the way down'. In Discussion the authors raise the opposite worry: an L1 penalty may push too far toward sparsity and so favor local codes over compositional ones.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Hyperparameter Selection

concepts.name: Learning Rate Sweep
concepts.summary: Trying multiple learning rates alongside varying training lengths. The paper reports lower learning rates, given enough steps, give lower loss and more real features.
concepts.explanation: The paper ran several training runs across learning rates while also varying the number of training steps, and found that lower learning rates with sufficient steps produced lower total loss and more 'real' features, judged by the [[feature-density]] histograms. It also tried annealing the learning rate over training and reports this gave no further improvement. Learning rate that is too high is separately listed as one of the factors that produces [[dead-neurons]].

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: Neuron Resampling
concepts.summary: Periodically reinitializing autoencoder neurons that have stopped firing, aiming them at datapoints the autoencoder currently reconstructs worst.
concepts.explanation: At training steps 25,000, 50,000, 75,000 and 100,000, the paper identifies neurons that have not fired in any of the previous 12,500 steps. It computes the autoencoder's loss on a random subset of 819,200 inputs and assigns each input a selection probability proportional to the square of that loss. For each dead neuron it samples an input, renormalizes it to unit L2 norm, and installs it as that neuron's dictionary vector; the encoder vector is set to the same direction scaled to 0.2 times the average encoder norm of live neurons, with the encoder bias element zeroed. Finally the Adam state for every modified parameter is reset. The paper says this beats both no resampling and a plain Kaiming Uniform reinitialization, and that better strategies are an active research area.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: Pre-Encoder Bias
concepts.summary: A bias subtracted from the input before the encoder, constrained to be the negative of the decoder's output bias. The paper lists it as its most important modification to a standard autoencoder.
concepts.explanation: The forward pass begins with $\bar{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{b}_d$, so the same learned vector is removed at the input and added back at the output. The effect is equivalent to subtracting a fixed offset from all activations and then running an autoencoder whose only bias sits before the encoder nonlinearity. The paper reports that on toy problems with a bias, the autoencoder failed to reproduce the expected diagnostic plots unless bias terms were added at both ends. It ranks this first in its rough ordering of modifications by importance, on the basis of toy-model performance rather than an ablation on the real model.

citedFrom.refText: Hobbhahn, Marius (2023). More findings on Memorization and double descent.
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The paper says these investigations were motivated by Hobbhahn's observations; the observation itself is not restated here.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: Scaling sparse autoencoders
concepts.summary: The open engineering problem of applying this method to frontier models, which the authors call one of the most important questions going forward.
concepts.explanation: Two costs dominate. Parameters: a 100× autoencoder on a single MLP layer of width 10,000 would have roughly 20 billion parameters. Data: many features are rare, so the autoencoder may need to be trained on a substantial fraction of the subject model's training corpus — potentially making the autoencoder more expensive than the model it explains. The authors are hopeful, pointing to Cunningham et al. and unreported preliminary results of their own, and note the silver lining that a large part of the interpretability agenda then becomes an engineering and scaling problem that frontier labs are equipped for.

concepts.name: Reconstruction Plus Sparsity Loss
concepts.summary: The training objective: mean squared reconstruction error plus an L1 penalty on the hidden activations, $\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|X|}\sum_\mathbf{x} \|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_2^2 + \lambda\|\mathbf{f}\|_1$.
concepts.explanation: Two terms pull against each other: the MSE term wants the reconstruction to be faithful, which is easiest with many features active, and the L1 term wants few features active, which costs reconstruction accuracy. Everything the method produces sits somewhere on that tradeoff, set by $\lambda$. The paper notes a convention that matters if you are reimplementing it: the MSE is a mean over vector elements while the L1 is a sum over feature activations. It also notes that using MSE rather than an architectural sparsity mechanism sidesteps the problems with architectural approaches it discussed earlier.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: Untied Decoder Weights
concepts.summary: The encoder weights are learned independently of the decoder weights rather than being constrained to their transpose. The paper reports the two end up meaningfully different.
concepts.explanation: The replicator reports that per-feature encoder and decoder weights are only moderately aligned, with median cosine similarity around 0.5 — empirical evidence they are doing different things. The conceptual argument given alongside it: the decoder tries to represent the feature, approximating the true direction regardless of interference, while the encoder tries to *detect* it, choosing the projection that best separates it from other similar features. Those are different optimization problems, so the weights should be allowed to differ.

citedFrom.refText: Cunningham, Hoagy and Ewart, Aidan and Smith, Logan and Huben, Robert and Sharkey, Lee. Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Model Directions. arXiv:2309.08600
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The tied-weight convention this paper departs from is established in these prior sparse autoencoder works; the comparison only makes sense against them.

sections.title: Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: MSE Reconstruction Term
concepts.summary: The squared error between the original MLP activation and the autoencoder's reconstruction, averaged over vector elements.
concepts.explanation: This term is what ties the learned features to the actual computation: if the reconstruction is poor, the features are not a description of what the MLP layer was doing. The paper uses it directly as one of its guiding metrics, on the grounds that the goal is to explain the MLP layer's function so the reconstruction error should be low. Note the asymmetry in normalization — mean over elements for MSE, sum for L1 — which fixes what a given $\lambda$ means numerically.

sections.title: How can we tell if the autoencoder is working?
Advice for Training Sparse Autoencoders: Autoencoder Architecture

concepts.name: Architectural approaches, and why they were abandoned
concepts.summary: The attempt to build models that simply do not have superposition, which the authors conclude is not merely costly but fundamentally non-viable for language models.
concepts.explanation: This was the approach the authors initially found cleanest: even if monosemantic models came with a large loss penalty, they would be useful research objects. After substantial investigation they concluded otherwise. Their experiments [[activation-sparsity-training|inducing activation sparsity during training]] — up to and including 1-hot activations — did eliminate superposition, but did not produce cleanly interpretable neurons. The reason is that polysemanticity can be preferred by a cross-entropy-trained model even with no superposition available, which is a separate failure from the one superposition causes.

concepts.name: Attentional superposition
concepts.summary: The open question of whether attention layers also use superposition, and whether similar methods would extract features from them.
concepts.explanation: Listed as future work. The authors note that many of the motivations for expecting superposition in MLP layers apply to self-attention layers too, so similar methods might extract useful structure there — but they say no clear example has yet been established. If attention layers do use superposition and resist these methods, that becomes a bottleneck for the wider agenda.

concepts.name: Disentanglement
concepts.summary: A related literature seeking representations whose dimensions separate conceptually distinct factors influencing the data — typically as many factors as dimensions, not more.
concepts.explanation: The contrast with superposition is dimensional. Disentanglement seeks a number of factors equal to the dimensionality of the representation; superposition holds that models want more features than dimensions and will pay to have them. Disentanglement work is usually posed as an architecture or training-time problem: encouraging independence across the dimensions of a variational autoencoder, maximizing mutual information between a subset of latent factors and the data in a GAN, or using a [[topk-activation]] to force sparsity. The paper places its own architectural attempts, including SoLU, inside this framing.

concepts.name: Feature sparsity
concepts.summary: The property that only a small number of the model's features are active on any given datapoint.
concepts.explanation: Sparsity is the precondition for superposition: if many features were active at once their interference would swamp the signal. In Toy Models the authors showed that superposition arises naturally during training when the useful features are sparse in the training data. Sparsity is also what the [[sparse-autoencoder]]'s L1 penalty is trying to reimpose on the learned decomposition. The paper is careful about the direction of the argument — sparsity in the data is what permits the representation, and sparsity in the objective is what lets you recover it.

concepts.name: Interference
concepts.summary: The cross-talk that arises because feature directions in superposition cannot all be orthogonal: activating one feature slightly activates others.
concepts.explanation: With more directions than dimensions, any two feature directions have nonzero dot product, so reading off one feature picks up a contribution from every other active feature. In Toy Models this pressure makes features 'repel' from each other, producing roughly evenly spaced directions. In this paper interference shows up empirically as 'interference weights': the broad, near-isotropic cloud of small logit effects a feature has on tokens it has nothing to do with. The authors count the existence of that cloud as evidence for superposition.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Memorization in superposition
concepts.summary: A prior finding that when a toy model is trained on repeated small datasets it memorizes datapoints in superposition rather than learning generalizing features.
concepts.explanation: The paper invokes this to explain features that appear to memorize specific phrases, such as the sequence of features covering 'MERCHANTABILITY or FITNESS FOR A PARTICULAR PURPOSE' — legal boilerplate that appears in open source license headers and so was seen many times in training. On that theory these features should be relatively binary and fire only in a very specific situation, which is what the authors report seeing. They add the caveat that mechanisms buried this deep in superposition are likely very noisy.

citedFrom.refText: Henighan, Tom et al. (2023). Superposition, Memorization, and Double Descent. Transformer Circuits Thread
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The mechanistic theory of memorization being applied to the observed phrase features is developed there, including the memorization/generalization boundary.

concepts.name: Noisy simulation of a larger network
concepts.summary: The mechanism proposed for superposition: a small network exploits feature sparsity and the geometry of high-dimensional spaces to approximately simulate a much larger, much sparser network.
concepts.explanation: The simulated network has one neuron per feature and is almost never more than a few neurons active. The small network packs those features into fewer dimensions along non-orthogonal directions; the resulting cross-talk is the 'noise' in noisy simulation. High-dimensional geometry helps because many directions can be nearly orthogonal at once, and sparsity helps because few features are simultaneously active to interfere. The paper draws the analogy to [[compressed-sensing]]: sparsity is what lets you disambiguate which combination of features produced a given activation vector.

concepts.name: Theories of superposition, revised
concepts.summary: The paper's reassessment of the picture it inherited: features clump into dense related groups and may not be one-dimensional, which the earlier toy picture did not anticipate.
concepts.explanation: Discussion opens by naming the inherited view — the isotropic model — and saying this work persuaded the authors it was missing something. At minimum, features clump into higher-density groups of related features. Two explanations are offered, correlated activations and shared downstream actions, with the second suspected to be more central. Beyond clumping, the authors question whether features are one-dimensional at all, raising higher-dimensional [[feature-manifolds]]. They note the hypotheses are not mutually exclusive: the convex hull of several [[correlated-features]] could be read as a manifold, though some manifolds would not admit any finite description in terms of one-dimensional features.

concepts.name: Three approaches to superposition
concepts.summary: The strategies laid out in Toy Models: build models without superposition, use dictionary learning on models that have it, or combine the two.
concepts.explanation: The authors report having tried all three since publishing Toy Models. They came to believe the architectural route (approach 1) is insufficient to prevent polysemanticity, for reasons given in Section 2.3, and that standard [[dictionary-learning]] methods (approach 2) had significant trouble with overfitting. The [[sparse-autoencoder]] is presented as a deliberately weak form of approach 2 chosen to avoid that overfitting.

concepts.name: Toy Models of Superposition
concepts.summary: The authors' earlier paper, which showed superposition arising in small synthetic models and supplied the theoretical picture this paper works from and revises.
concepts.explanation: Toy Models established that superposition arises naturally in training when features are sparse, catalogued geometric arrangements of feature directions, and proposed the three approaches to resolving superposition. This paper inherits its vocabulary and its predictions, then reports two places where it fell short: it treated features as discrete one-dimensional objects spread evenly apart, and although it studied features correlated in *whether* they fire, it had nothing analogous to features that share downstream actions. The authors conclude the toy picture is 'missing an important dimension of the problem'.

citedFrom.refText: Elhage, Nelson et al. (2022). Toy Models of Superposition. Transformer Circuits Thread
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The superposition hypothesis, the noisy-simulation picture, the isotropic geometry, and the three approaches are all defined there and assumed here without re-derivation.

concepts.name: Action-sharing features
concepts.summary: Features that produce similar downstream effects and therefore end up with similar directions — the paper's suspected main cause of feature clustering.
concepts.explanation: The worked case: the feature firing on single digits in base64 predicts approximately the same set of tokens as the feature firing on other base64 characters, except for other digits. Similar downstream effects manifest as geometrically close feature directions, because producing similar output actions requires producing similar neuron activations. Combined with the features also being highly correlated in when they fire, this gives real models both denser and more structured superposition than the toy models predicted. Toy Models did study [[correlated-features]], but only correlation in whether they are active, with no analogue of shared output actions.

concepts.name: Is there a correct number of features?
concepts.summary: Under some expanded theories the question is not well posed; under others there is a true number but getting it exactly right is not essential.
concepts.explanation: The paper separates two cases. If features form continuous manifolds, asking for the correct count may have no answer. If there is a true finite set, the consequence of getting the count wrong is mild — the process 'fails gracefully', showing the [[true-features]] at different granularities as the dictionary grows. Either way the practical upshot is the same: dictionary size is a resolution knob rather than a parameter that must be tuned correctly.

concepts.name: Correlated features
concepts.summary: Features that tend to fire together, offered as one explanation for why feature directions clump.
concepts.explanation: This is the explanation the authors consider less central than shared actions, though they note the two are not exclusive. Toy Models had examined correlated features, including how correlation organizes feature directions and how strongly correlated features can collapse into a single broader feature. The paper flags that collapsing-versus-tight-superposition distinction as the useful intuition to carry over: two similar features held separately in tight superposition is a different situation from one broader feature.

concepts.name: Feature manifolds
concepts.summary: The possibility that some features are not one-dimensional intensity scales but higher-dimensional continuous families of related directions.
concepts.explanation: The inherited picture has each feature encoding only an intensity along a fixed direction. The paper raises the alternative that a set of related features forms a continuous surface in activation space. The convex hull of several [[correlated-features]] could be understood this way, but the authors note the reverse does not hold: some manifolds would not admit a unique description in terms of any finite number of one-dimensional features. They suggest this might account for the continued [[feature-splitting]] they observe — if the underlying object is continuous, no finite dictionary ever finishes resolving it.

concepts.name: Isotropic superposition model
concepts.summary: The inherited picture from Toy Models: features are discrete, one-dimensional, and repel each other through interference into a roughly evenly spaced arrangement of directions.
concepts.explanation: Each of its three commitments is questioned by this work. Discrete and one-dimensional is challenged by [[feature-manifolds]] and by [[feature-splitting]] that never seems to stop. Evenly spaced is challenged directly by the observed clusters of features with small angles between directions. The paper does not discard the model — it says the experiments left it more confident that some version of superposition is true — but concludes the toy models work is missing an important dimension of the problem by not studying highly correlated, [[action-sharing-features|action-sharing features]].

concepts.name: Activation similarity
concepts.summary: The procedure for finding a feature's counterpart in another dictionary: take the feature with the highest Pearson correlation of activations over 40,960,000 tokens.
concepts.explanation: The idea is to treat a feature as a function assigning values to datapoints; two features are similar if they take similar values over diverse data. This gives a representation that does not depend on either model's internal coordinates, so features from different models can be compared directly. For each feature in A/1 the paper finds the closest feature in B/1 by this measure and reports a median correlation of 0.72. Features with low correlation may reflect different splittings in the two dictionaries, or genuinely different [[true-features]] in the two base models.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Attribution similarity
concepts.summary: A third comparison measure that weights a feature's logit effects by whether the feature was actually active and the token actually came next.
concepts.explanation: It is introduced to get at 'the actual effect a feature has on token probabilities' without the cost of full ablations. The paper finds attribution similarity correlates quite highly with [[activation-similarity]], meaning features that were coactive across models were useful for predicting the same tokens. That result is what licenses using the cheaper activation correlation as the paper's default universality measure — it stands in for both notions of similarity in this one-layer setting.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Logit weight similarity
concepts.summary: Comparing features by what they do rather than when they fire: correlate their logit weight vectors, indexed by vocabulary token.
concepts.explanation: This is the downstream-effects counterpart to [[activation-similarity]], and in a one-layer model logit weights are a cheap approximation to a feature's effect on predictions. The paper finds the two measures often disagree. For the Arabic feature, the activation correlation between models is 0.91 while the [[logit-weight]] correlation is only 0.23: both models upweight the Arabic-script tokens, but the large cloud of small effects on other tokens looks like isotropic noise and drags the correlation down. The paper reports this disagreement is widespread.

sections.title: Comparing features between two one-layer transformers

concepts.name: Matching features to the literature
concepts.summary: A stronger universality test: checking whether features found here resemble units reported in other models by other researchers.
concepts.explanation: The paper finds base64, hexadecimal and all-caps features matching neurons it previously found in one-layer SoLU models, which use a different activation function. It finds a German detector and title case detectors matching features another group found by applying [[dictionary-learning]] to a residual stream, along with the same preponderance of single-token features. It finds a 'prime factors' feature and a French feature matching results from [[sparse-probing]]. Matches to multimodal vision-language models are looser — region features for Australia, Canada, Africa and Israel-Palestine loosely mirror reported region neurons, person detectors appear only in very narrow contexts, and no clear analogue of emotion neurons is found.

concepts.name: Multimodal neurons
concepts.summary: Units in vision-language models reported to respond to a concept across images and text, including region, person and emotion neurons.
concepts.explanation: The paper uses these as the most distant comparison point for universality. Region neurons find loose analogues among its features. Person detector neurons — themselves compared to famous single-neuron results in neuroscience — do not: the paper finds features that detect people only in very narrow contexts, such as responding to a name and predicting appropriate next words. No clear analogue of emotion neurons is found. This is one of the places where the paper reports a negative result plainly.

citedFrom.refText: Goh, Gabriel et al. (2021). Multimodal Neurons in Artificial Neural Networks. Distill
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The specific neuron families being matched against — region, person, emotion neurons — and what evidence established them are defined there.

concepts.name: Sparse probing
concepts.summary: Training sparse linear probes on activations to find whether a property is represented, and by how few neurons.
concepts.explanation: Cited twice: as independent evidence that features may be in superposition, and as a source of features this paper matches — a prime factors feature and a French feature. Sparse probing is a top-down method: you must know what property to probe for. That contrast is part of why the paper values the bottom-up [[dictionary-learning]] approach, which surfaced distinctions like the three kinds of base64 that nobody would have thought to probe for.

citedFrom.refText: Gurnee, Wes and Nanda, Neel and Pauly, Matthew and Harvey, Katherine and Troitskii, Dmitrii and Bertsimas, Dimitris. Finding Neurons in a Haystack: Case Studies with Sparse Probing. arXiv:2305.01610
citedFrom.whyNeeded: The probing method and the specific features found there are what the universality comparison is being made against.

concepts.name: Encoder Tilt Against Crosstalk
concepts.summary: The paper's account of why untying helps: features with similar dictionary vectors get encoder vectors tilted away from each other, so they can be told apart.
concepts.explanation: When two features write along nearly the same direction, a tied encoder would read them nearly identically and confuse them. The paper reports that in its trained autoencoders the encoder vectors for such features, while still similar, are tilted further apart than the dictionary vectors, which it reads as preventing crosstalk between noisy feature inputs. The worked case is [[base64-feature-family|the three base64 features]] described elsewhere in the paper, which share similar dictionary vectors but have more separated encoder vectors. This is offered as intuition backed by an example, not a quantitative result.

concepts.name: Hypothesis 3: The Autoencoder Is Imperfect
concepts.summary: If the dictionary is narrower than the number of true features, the missing features may show up smeared as weak activations across many learned ones.
concepts.explanation: If the model uses more [[true-features]] than the autoencoder has capacity to represent, the unrecovered ones have to go somewhere. The paper's suggestion is that they appear as low activations spread across many learned features, contaminating the bottom of every activation spectrum. This links the specificity story to the general question of how many features the dictionary is missing, which section 4.2 and the density histograms take up.

concepts.name: Hypothesis 2: The Model Is Imperfect But Calibrated
concepts.summary: If features activate in proportion to the model's confidence that a property holds, weak activations should sometimes be wrong.
concepts.explanation: On this reading a feature's activation is something like a confidence, and a calibrated confidence is supposed to be wrong some of the time when it is low. The paper concedes it seems silly for a model to be unsure what language a passage is in, but points out that this is a very weak one-layer transformer and that characters split across multiple tokens make the task harder than it looks. Under this hypothesis the low activations are correct behavior, not noise.

concepts.name: Hypothesis 1: The Proxy Is Imperfect
concepts.summary: Weak activations may look impure because the proxy misses characters that are genuinely part of the context.
concepts.explanation: The Arabic proxy scores by Unicode block, so common characters shared across scripts — whitespace, punctuation, newlines — score low even inside Arabic text. The paper gives a concrete case from its own figure: a newline character the feature fires on but the proxy scores low because it is outside the Arabic block. Odd tokenizer behavior contributes as well. Under this hypothesis the feature is fine and the yardstick is bent.
